rules.title: Reimburse all necessary work expenses and losses (Labor Code 2802)
rules.plain_english: If a worker spends their own money or loses property because they did the job or followed your instructions, you must pay them back. Examples include required insurance, bank fees for required direct deposit, required uniforms and business use of a personal vehicle.

parameters.reimburse: all necessary expenditures or losses incurred in direct consequence of the discharge of duties or obedience to the employer's directions
parameters.test: expense or loss incurred within the course and scope of employment (respondeat superior)
examples_per_dlse: cost of opening or operating a bank account required for direct deposit (O.L. 1997.03.21-2)
business use of the employee's car (mileage)
legal costs of defending a third-party action based on job-related conduct
employee-owned tools stolen from the employer's premises when trade custom required the employee to supply them and they were too heavy to carry home

rules.applies_to: All California employers
rules.quote: An employer shall indemnify his or her employee for all necessary expenditures of losses incurred by the employee in direct consequence of the discharge of his or her duties, or of his or her obedience to the directions of the employer, even though unlawful, unless the employee, at the time of obeying the directions, believed them to be unlawful.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from July 2017 to December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. The manual's wording 'expenditures of losses' is copied as printed. The DLSE Deductions FAQ (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_Deductions.htm) says the same in plain terms: 'An employee is entitled to be reimbursed by his or her employer for all expenses or losses incurred in the direct consequence of the discharge of the employee's work duties.'
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. The uniforms example is in the Deductions FAQ, item d, which the notes cite. It is not in manual ch. 29.

rules.title: Mileage: the IRS rate is presumed reasonable, but higher actual costs must be covered
rules.plain_english: When workers drive their own vehicles for work, paying the IRS mileage rate normally satisfies the law. If a worker proves their real costs were higher, for example because you require extra insurance, you must pay the difference. Paying less than the IRS rate is presumed not to comply unless you prove actual costs were lower.

parameters.presumed_reasonable_rate: IRS business standard mileage rate for the period driven
parameters.below_irs_rate: rebuttably presumed not to comply; employer may show actual costs were lower
parameters.at_irs_rate: no irrebuttable presumption; employee may prove higher actual costs
parameters.employer_required_extra_auto_insurance: reimbursable; employer may not dictate the insurance company (Labor Code 450)

rules.applies_to: Employers whose employees use personal vehicles for work (travel between jobsites, supply runs)
rules.citation: Labor Code 2802; DLSE Enforcement Manual §29.2.4; DLSE Opinion Letter 1998.11.05
rules.quote: DLSE has opined that use of the IRS mileage allowance will satisfy the expenses incurred in use of an employee’s car in the absence of evidence to the contrary.
rules.notes: The 1998 opinion letter adds: 'Thus while the Division generally finds the IRS mileage rate as reimbursement to be reasonable, no overall exemption from liability under Section 2802 can be given.' It also says payments below the IRS rate were 'rebuttably presumed not to comply with Section 2802.' The 2026 and 2027 IRS mileage rates were not read because irs.gov is blocked here, so a calculator must take the rate as an input.

rules.title: Expenses can be built into pay only with a stated formula
rules.plain_english: You may cover expenses with a higher wage or commission rate only if you show how much of each payment is expense reimbursement, so the worker can check that wages and expenses were both fully paid.

parameters.allowed_method: increase base salary or commission rates to cover expenses
parameters.condition: employer provides a method or formula identifying the reimbursement portion of the combined payment
parameters.authority: Gattuso v. Harte-Hanks Shoppers, Inc. (2007) 42 Cal.4th 554, 573

rules.applies_to: All California employers
rules.quote: The California Supreme Court held an employer could satisfy the reimbursement obligation by increasing base salary or commission rates to meet its reimbursement obligation under Labor Code §2802 only where the employer provides some method or formula to identify the amount of the combined employee compensation payment that is intended to provide for expense reimbursement
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from July 2017. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.

rules.title: 'Hand tools' that workers may be required to supply exclude power tools and vehicles
rules.plain_english: Under the wage order, workers who earn at least twice the minimum wage can be required to bring the hand tools customary in their trade. That covers hand tools and tool belts or boxes only. It does not cover power tools or a car, which you must supply or reimburse.

hand_tools_and_equipment_includes: personal equipment such as tool belts or tool boxes needed to secure the hand tools
parameters.must_be: customarily required in a recognized trade or craft

rules.applies_to: Construction employers requiring workers to supply tools
rules.citation: IWC Order 16-2001 §8(B); Labor Code 2802; DLSE Enforcement Manual §§29.2.3.2-29.2.3.3
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§29.2.3.2 and §29.2.3.3, manual pages 29-2 to 29-3); https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle16.pdf (§8(B) UNIFORMS AND EQUIPMENT: wages at least two (2) times the minimum wage); 2027 rate: https://www.dir.ca.gov/DIRNews/2026/2026-66.html
rules.quote: The DLSE has concluded that in the phrase “hand tools and equipment”, the word “hand” is an adjective which modifies both the word “tools” and the word “equipment”. As the Labor Commissioner opined in 1984, an automobile is not the type of equipment contemplated in the IWC Orders.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages are dated July 2017 (29-2) and December 2020 (29-3). That quotation runs across a page break, so it is summarized here.
rules.correction: source_location now also names IWC Order 16 §8(B), the source of the 2x-minimum-wage condition. The citation already named it, but source_location did not. It also names News Release 2026-66, the source of the $17.40 behind the derived 2027 figure of $34.80. The notes' page date was corrected: p. 29-3 is dated December 2020, not July 2017. No parameter changed.

rules.title: Pay any bank costs when you require direct deposit
rules.plain_english: If you make workers open a bank account so they can be paid by direct deposit, you must cover the cost of opening and running that account.

parameters.employer_pays: any cost of opening or operating a bank account the employer requires for direct deposit

rules.applies_to: Employers requiring direct deposit
rules.quote: For instance, if an employer requires that an employee open a bank account in order to receive his or her pay by direct deposit, the employer must pay the employee for any cost involved in opening or operating that bank account.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from July 2017. rules.title: Training needed for a state-required license is usually not the employer's cost
rules.plain_english: Under Labor Commissioner policy, an employer usually does not have to pay for training a worker takes to earn a license that the law requires.

parameters.scope: training leading to licensure pursuant to a statute

rules.applies_to: All California employers
rules.quote: Costs which are incurred in training leading to licensure pursuant to a statute (real estate, etc.) are not, usually, the responsibility of the employer. (O.L. 1994.11.17)

rules.title: 2802 claims: employee recovers interest and attorney's fees; the right cannot be waived
rules.plain_english: A worker who wins an expense-reimbursement claim also gets interest and attorney's fees. An agreement in which a worker gives up reimbursement is not valid.
rules.applies_to: All California employers
rules.quote: Both interest and attorney’s fees incurred in claims and actions to enforce 2802 are recoverable and may be awarded by either the courts or the Labor Commissioner to an employee (but not the DLSE or employer) who prevails in such an enforcement claim or action. (Labor Code § 2802(c))
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited page (29-3) is dated December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. §29.2.6: 'Note: The provisions of Labor Code § 2800 and 2802 may not be altered or waived by private agreement. (Labor Code § 2804)'.

rules.title: Only three kinds of paycheck deductions are allowed
rules.plain_english: You may take money out of a paycheck only when the law requires it (taxes, garnishments), when the worker agreed in writing to pay for things like insurance or benefit plans, or when a union or wage agreement authorizes health, welfare or pension contributions.

allowed_deductions: required or empowered by state or federal law (e.g., income taxes, garnishments)
expressly authorized in writing by the employee for insurance premiums, benefit plan contributions or other deductions not amounting to a rebate on wages
health, welfare or pension contributions expressly authorized by a wage or collective bargaining agreement

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: An employer can lawfully withhold amounts from an employee's wages only: (1) when required or empowered to do so by state or federal law, or (2) when a deduction is expressly authorized in writing by the employee to cover insurance premiums, benefit plan contributions or other deductions not amounting to a rebate on the employee's wages, or (3) when a deduction to cover health, welfare, or pension contributions is expressly authorized by a wage or collective bargaining agreement

rules.title: No paycheck deductions for accidents, breakage or lost equipment
rules.plain_english: You cannot dock pay for damaged tools, broken equipment or cash shortages caused by an accident or simple carelessness. The only exception is a loss you can prove came from dishonesty, a willful act or gross negligence, and even then the deduction is at your own risk.

parameters.deduction_allowed_only_if: employer proves the loss was caused by a dishonest or willful act or gross negligence
parameters.simple_negligence_or_accident: employer bears the loss as a cost of doing business
if_deduction_later_found_wrongful: former employee may also recover Labor Code 203 waiting time penalty

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 224; IWC Orders (cash shortage, breakage, loss of equipment section); DLSE Deductions FAQ Q2
rules.quote: No, your employer cannot legally make such a deduction from your wages if, by reason of mistake or accident a cash shortage, breakage, or loss of company property/equipment occurs.
rules.notes: DLSE warns that the wage-order exception for dishonest, willful or grossly negligent losses 'may, in fact, not comply with the provisions of the California Labor Code and various California Court decisions.'

rules.title: Final paycheck: deduct only one loan installment, not the whole balance
rules.plain_english: If a worker is repaying a loan from you through payroll, you may take only one regular installment from the final paycheck, even if the worker signed an agreement allowing more.

parameters.balloon_deduction_at_separation: not permitted even with written consent

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 221, 224; Barnhill v. Sanders (1981) 125 Cal.App.3d 1; DLSE Deductions FAQ Q4
rules.quote: When the employment relationship ends, your employer can only deduct the amount of one installment payment from your final paycheck.

rules.title: Docking pay for lateness: up to the time lost, or a half hour if late under 30 minutes
rules.plain_english: You may dock pay for lateness, but no more than the pay for the time actually missed. If the worker is less than 30 minutes late, you may dock up to a half hour.

parameters.max_deduction: proportionate wage for the time actually lost

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 2928; DLSE Deductions FAQ Q5
rules.quote: The deduction shall not, however, exceed the proportionate wage that would have been earned during the time actually lost, but for a loss of time less than 30 minutes, a half hour's wage may be deducted.

rules.title: Employer pays for any bond or photograph it requires
rules.plain_english: If you require an applicant or worker to be bonded or to provide a photo, you must pay for it.

employer_pays: bond required of an applicant or employee
photograph required of an applicant or employee

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors

rules.title: No firing because wages are garnished for one judgment
rules.plain_english: You must process a wage garnishment. You cannot fire a worker because a garnishment was threatened or because their wages are being garnished for one judgment.

protected: garnishment for payment of one judgment

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors

rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_Deductions.htm (introduction); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (ch. 17, Labor Code section 2929(b) and (c), manual page 17-12)

rules.title: Employer pays for medical exams it requires, and for exams the law requires of current employees
rules.plain_english: You cannot charge an applicant for a pre-employment physical you require. You also cannot charge a current worker, or deduct from pay, for any medical exam the law requires. An applicant may be asked to pay only for a pre-employment exam that the law itself requires.

rules.title: Victim absences: a signed statement from the worker is enough proof
rules.plain_english: If a crime victim misses work without notice, you cannot act against them if they give proof within a reasonable time afterward. A signed written statement from the worker counts as proof. This is the Labor Code 230 and 230.1 rule, which covers violations through December 31, 2024. Since January 1, 2025 crime-victim protections are under the Fair Employment and Housing Act (Gov. Code 12945.8), handled by the Civil Rights Department; its current proof rule was not checked.

parameters.unscheduled_absence_protected_if: certification provided within a reasonable time after the absence
accepted_certification: documentation from a licensed medical professional, domestic violence counselor, sexual assault counselor, licensed health care provider, victim advocate or counselor
signed written statement by the employee or someone acting for the employee
parameters.governing_law_after_cutover: Fair Employment and Housing Act, Gov. Code 12945.8 (Civil Rights Department); text not read

rules.citation: Labor Code 230(d)(2), 230.1(b)(2) (through 2024-12-31); Gov. Code 12945.8 (from 2025-01-01); DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4

rules.title: Parents may take time off when a teacher asks them to come to school
rules.plain_english: If a worker's child's teacher asks the parent or guardian to come to school, you must let them go if they give you reasonable notice first.

parameters.trigger: request of the pupil's teacher (Education Code 48900.1)
parameters.employee_must_give: reasonable notice before taking the time off

rules.applies_to: California employers (no size threshold is stated in the sources read)
rules.citation: Labor Code 230.7; Education Code 48900.1; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code section 230.7, manual page 17-5); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm (230.7 entry, page dated June 2026)
rules.quote: Protects an employee who is the parent or guardian of a pupil for taking time off from work to appear in the pupil’s school at the request of the pupil’s teacher, if the employee, prior to taking the time off, gives reasonable notice to the employer that he or she is requested to appear at the school.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.
rules.correction: min_employees changed from 1 to null and applies_to from 'All California employers (any size)' to 'no size threshold is stated'. Neither the manual nor DIR's June 2026 list states a size rule for 230.7. A '1' is not in the text. Added the June 2026 list to source_location. Quote and notice rule confirmed.

rules.title: Employers with 25+ employees at the same location: up to 40 hours a year for school activities (8 hours a month)
rules.plain_english: If you have 25 or more employees working at the same location, parents, guardians, stepparents, foster parents and grandparents may take up to 40 hours a year, and no more than 8 hours in a month, for their child's school activities or to find, enroll or re-enroll the child in school or licensed child care, after giving reasonable notice. The monthly limit does not apply to child care or school emergencies.

purposes: participate in activities of the child's school
locate, enroll or reenroll the child in school or with a licensed child care provider
child care provider or school emergencies
parameters.employee_count_basis: 25 or more employees working at the same location

rules.applies_to: California employers with 25 or more employees working at the same location
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code section 230.8, manual page 17-5); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm (230.8 entry, page dated June 2026)
rules.quote: Protects an employee who is a parent (including stepparent, foster parent, or person who stands in loco parentis to the child), guardian, or grandparent, and who is employed by an employer who employs 25 or more employees, for taking time off from work (up to 40 hours each year, not exceeding eight hours in any calendar month) to participate in activities of the child’s school, or to locate or enroll the child in school or with a child care provider or for school emergencies (no eight hour restriction for school emergencies.)
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. Notice and pay rules (for example, use of vacation) are in the statute, which was not read. Verification 2026-11-25: DIR's June 2026 list counts '25 or more employees working at the same location', adds re-enrollment and licensed child care providers, and covers child care provider emergencies as well as school emergencies.
rules.correction: Scope and purposes updated to DIR's newer June 2026 list. The headcount is '25 or more employees working at the same location' (the 2020 manual says only 'employs 25 or more'). The purposes now include reenrolling and licensed child care providers, and the emergency carve-out covers child care provider and school emergencies. Added employee_count_basis and notice. Title, plain_english, applies_to, source_location and notes updated. The 25, 40 and 8 figures are confirmed by both sources.

rules.title: Volunteer firefighters and reserve officers may take time off for emergency duty
rules.plain_english: Workers who are volunteer firefighters, reserve peace officers or emergency rescue personnel are protected when they take time off for emergency duty. Health care workers must tell you when they are designated and when they are deployed.

covered: emergency rescue personnel (the December 2020 manual words this as an officer, employee or member of a disaster medical response entity sponsored or requested by the State)
parameters.health_care_provider_notice: notify employer when designated as emergency rescue personnel and when notified of deployment because of that designation

rules.applies_to: California employers (the source does not state a size threshold)
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code section 230.3, manual page 17-4); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm (230.3 entry, page dated June 2026)
rules.quote: Protects an employee who takes time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or an officer, employee, or member of a disaster medical response entity sponsored or requested by the State.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.
rules.correction: covered and health_care_provider_notice updated to DIR's newer June 2026 wording: 'volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel'; health care providers notify when designated as emergency rescue personnel and when deployed. The manual's disaster-medical-response wording is kept as a parenthetical. plain_english and source_location updated. min_employees stays null (no size stated).

rules.title: Employers with 50+ employees: up to 14 days a year for fire, law enforcement or emergency rescue training
rules.plain_english: If you have 50 or more employees, volunteer firefighters, reserve peace officers and emergency rescue workers may take up to 14 days a year for fire, law enforcement or emergency rescue training.

parameters.purpose: fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training

rules.applies_to: California employers with 50 or more employees
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code section 230.4, manual page 17-4); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm (230.4 entry, page dated June 2026)
rules.quote: Protects an employee who is a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel, and works for an employer employing 50 or more employees, from being discriminated or retaliated against because he or she has taken time off to engage in fire or law enforcement training. The employee is permitted to take up to an aggregate of 14 days per calendar year for such training.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.
rules.correction: purpose widened from 'fire or law enforcement training' to 'fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training' per DIR's June 2026 list. plain_english and source_location updated. The 50-employee and 14-day figures are confirmed by both sources. Rewording 2026-11-27: title reworded to match this correction (DLSE list https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm re-read on 2026-11-27); no value changed.

rules.title: Employers with 25+ employees: accommodate workers entering alcohol or drug rehab
rules.plain_english: If you regularly employ 25 or more people, you must reasonably accommodate a worker who voluntarily enters an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program, usually with time off, unless it causes undue hardship. The time off can be unpaid, but the worker may use sick leave, and you must keep it private.

parameters.accommodation: reasonable accommodation (time off) to voluntarily enter and participate in a rehabilitation program

rules.applies_to: Private California employers regularly employing 25 or more employees
rules.citation: Labor Code 1025-1028; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4 and §26.3
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code sections 1025-1028, manual page 17-8; §§26.3-26.3.4, manual page 26-1)
rules.quote: Every private employer regularly employing 25 or more employees shall provide reasonable accommodations for an employee to participate in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages are dated April 2021 (17-8) and December 2020 (26-1). The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. The manual is inconsistent on the headcount: §17.1.4 says '25 or more', while §26.3 says 'more than 25'. The parameters use 25 or more. §26.3.3 says the employer is not responsible for paying for these absences but the employee may use sick leave. §26.3.2 requires reasonable efforts to keep enrollment private. Verification 2026-11-25: DIR's June 2026 list (Labor Code 1025-1028) says 'a private employer regularly employing 25 or more employees', which settles the manual's inconsistency in favor of 25 or more.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. The notes were edited: p. 17-8 is dated April 2021. They now record that DIR's June 2026 list says '25 or more', which resolves the 25-or-more versus more-than-25 inconsistency in the manual.

rules.title: Employers with 25+ employees: help workers who ask to enroll in adult literacy classes
rules.plain_english: If you regularly employ 25 or more people and a worker tells you they have trouble reading and asks for help enrolling in an adult literacy program, you must reasonably accommodate them and keep it private. You do not have to pay for the time off.

parameters.trigger: employee reveals a problem of illiteracy and requests assistance

rules.applies_to: Private California employers regularly employing 25 or more employees
rules.citation: Labor Code 1041-1044; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4 and §26.4
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code sections 1041-1044, manual page 17-10; §§26.4-26.4.2, manual pages 26-1 to 26-2); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm (1041-1044 entry, page dated June 2026)
rules.quote: Every private employer regularly employing 25 or more employees shall reasonably accommodate and assist any employee who reveals a problem of illiteracy and requests the employer’s assistance in enrolling in an adult literacy education program.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages are dated December 2017 (17-10), December 2020 (26-1) and August 2017 (26-2). The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. §26.4 says 'more than 25 employees', while §17.1.4 says '25 or more'. Verification 2026-11-25: DIR's June 2026 list says 'a private employer regularly employing 25 or more employees', which settles the inconsistency in favor of 25 or more.
rules.correction: source_location page corrected: the 1041-1044 entry is on manual p. 17-10, not 17-9. Added the 26-1 to 26-2 pages and the June 2026 DLSE list, which confirms '25 or more'. The page dates in the notes were corrected. No parameter changed.

rules.title: Organ and bone marrow donors are entitled to paid leave; no retaliation
rules.plain_english: Workers have a right to a paid leave of absence to donate an organ or bone marrow, and you cannot retaliate against them for taking it.
rules.applies_to: California employers (size threshold and day limits are in the statute, which was not read)
rules.quote: Prohibits retaliation against an employee who exercises the right to take a paid leave of absence for the purpose of donating his or her organ or bone marrow to another person
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. The employer-size threshold, the number of days and the rules on using other leave are in Labor Code 1508-1511, which this pass could not read. They are left as null.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. 'Paid' rests on the manual. DIR's June 2026 list says 'leave of absence' without 'paid' but does not contradict it. The size threshold and day limits remain null because Labor Code 1508-1511 was not read.

rules.title: Have a written lactation accommodation policy and hand it out
rules.plain_english: You need a written lactation policy in your handbook. Give it to new hires and to anyone who asks about or requests parental leave. It must state four things listed in the parameters.

distribute: when an employee inquires about or requests parental leave
include in employee handbook or set of policies made available to employees
required_contents: employee's right to request a lactation accommodation
employer must respond in writing if it cannot provide compliant break time or location
employee's right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 1034; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4 (Labor Code 1030-1034)
rules.quote: Employers are required to develop and implement a policy regarding lactation accommodation. The policy must be provided to employees upon hire, when an employee makes an inquiry about or requests parental leave and the policy must be included in an employee handbook or set of policies that the employer makes available to employees.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from April 2021. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. This extends the existing rule lactation-accommodation, which covers break time and the $100/day citation.

rules.title: Lactation space: private, not a bathroom, with a seat, surface, power, and nearby sink and fridge
rules.plain_english: The lactation space must not be a bathroom. It must be near the work area, private and free from intrusion, safe, clean and free of hazardous materials, with a place to sit, a surface for a pump and power. A sink with running water and a refrigerator must be nearby.

must_contain: surface for breast pump and personal items
electricity or alternative devices (extension cords, charging stations)
parameters.temporary_location_allowed_if: operational, financial or space limitations prevent a permanent location (still not a bathroom and otherwise compliant)

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 1031; DLSE Lactation Accommodation FAQ Q4; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4
rules.quote: The lactation room or location must be safe, clean, and free from hazardous materials, as defined in Labor Code section 6382, contain a surface to place a breast pump and personal items, contain a place to sit and have access to electricity or alternative devices, including but not limited to, extension cords or charging stations needed to operate an electric or battery-powered breast pump.
rules.notes: The FAQ page is dated April 2021. The temporary-location rule is from manual page 17-9.

rules.title: General contractors: provide lactation space for a subcontractor within 2 business days of a written request
rules.plain_english: On a multi-employer jobsite, the general contractor or coordinating employer must provide a lactation space, or a safe and secure spot where the subcontractor can set one up, within 2 business days after the subcontractor asks in writing.

parameters.trigger: written request of a subcontractor employer
parameters.obligated: employers or general contractors coordinating a multiemployer worksite
parameters.must_provide: lactation accommodations, or a safe and secure location for the subcontractor to provide them on the worksite
parameters.shared_space_allowed: multitenant or multiemployer worksite may share space if employer cannot provide one in its own workspace

rules.applies_to: General contractors and other employers coordinating multiemployer construction worksites
rules.quote: Employers or general contractors coordinating a multiemployer worksite must provide lactations accommodations or a safe and secure location for a subcontractor employer to provide the lactation accommodations on the worksite within two business days upon written request of a subcontractor employer.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from April 2021. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. 'lactations' is copied as printed.

rules.title: Employers under 50 employees may claim undue hardship for lactation breaks or space
rules.plain_english: An employer with fewer than 50 employees does not have to give lactation break time if it would cause significant difficulty or expense. If a compliant room would be an undue hardship, it must still make reasonable efforts to provide a private place that is not a toilet stall.

parameters.break_time_exemption: if undue hardship (significant difficulty or expense relative to size, financial resources, nature or structure)
parameters.room_fallback: reasonable efforts to provide a room or other location other than a toilet stall

rules.applies_to: California employers with fewer than 50 employees
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, 'Exception for Employer with less than 50 employees', manual page 17-9)
rules.quote: An employer with less than 50 employees is not required to provide an employee break time for purposes of expressing milk if to do so would impose an undue hardship by causing the employer significant difficulty or expense, when considered in relation to size, financial resources, nature, or structure of the employer’s business.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from April 2021. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.

rules.title: Do not require a doctor's note for lactation breaks
rules.plain_english: You cannot require a worker to give a doctor's note or any other paperwork to prove they need to express breast milk.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 1030; DLSE Lactation Accommodation FAQ Q3
rules.quote: No. Your employer cannot require you to submit any documentation regarding your need to express breast milk.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated April 2021.

rules.title: Workers may discuss and disclose wages; no gag rules or waivers
rules.plain_english: You cannot forbid workers from talking about their own pay or asking about co-workers' pay, and you cannot make them sign anything giving up that right.

protected_acts: aiding or encouraging others to exercise Equal Pay Act rights

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 232, 1102.5(a), 1197.5(k)(1); DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQ 'Can an employer prohibit an employee from talking about wages...')
rules.quote: No, an employer cannot prohibit an employee from disclosing the employee’s own wages, discussing the wages of others, inquiring about another employee’s wages, or aiding or encouraging any other employee to exercise their Equal Pay Act rights.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026. The same page says no law requires an employer to tell an employee what others are paid.

rules.title: Workers may discuss working conditions; NDAs cannot waive this
rules.plain_english: You cannot require workers to keep quiet about working conditions or to sign a waiver of that right. Confidentiality and non-disclosure agreements cannot override it.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 232.5; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4 and §26.1
rules.quote: Prohibits an employer from requiring that an employee refrain from disclosing or discussing information about the employer’s working conditions, and from requiring an employee to sign a waiver or other document that restricts or denies the employee the right to disclose or discuss information about the employer’s working conditions.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. §26.1: 'Any confidentiality, non-compete, or non-disclosure agreement, which limits or restricts what information an employee may discuss or disclose, may not waive or infringe on these statutory protections.'

rules.title: Do not ask about or use arrests without conviction, diversion, or dismissed or sealed convictions
rules.plain_english: When hiring or making job decisions, you cannot ask about or use arrests that did not lead to a conviction, diversion programs, or convictions that were dismissed or sealed. Applicants also do not have to disclose juvenile records.

may_not_seek_or_use: arrest or detention not resulting in conviction
referral to or participation in pretrial or posttrial diversion
conviction judicially dismissed or ordered sealed
conviction_questions_only_when: employer required by law to obtain conviction information
law bars a person with the conviction from the position
employer prohibited by law from hiring a person with the conviction

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code section 432.7, manual pages 17-6 to 17-7)
rules.quote: Prohibits an employer from seeking or using as a factor in an employment decision, any record of an arrest or detention that did not result in a conviction or any information regarding referral to, and participation in, any pretrial or posttrial diversion program or concerning a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. The Fair Chance Act (Gov. Code 12952, enforced by the Civil Rights Department) adds rules on when and how employers may consider convictions. Its text and the CRD guidance could not be read (leginfo and calcivilrights.ca.gov are blocked), so it is not encoded here.

rules.title: Do not ask about marijuana possession convictions more than 2 years old
rules.plain_english: Applicants and workers do not have to disclose a marijuana possession conviction that is more than two years old.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Protects the rights of an applicant for employment or employee from disclosing information regarding a conviction related to the possession of marijuana where the conviction is more than two years old.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. The 2-year figure is in the manual. DIR's June 2026 list describes 432.8 only as extending 432.7 to 'certain marijuana related convictions', which neither confirms nor contradicts it.

rules.title: No consumer credit reports for hiring, except listed positions
rules.plain_english: You cannot pull a credit report on an applicant or worker unless the job is an exempt managerial position under Wage Order 4 or falls into another category the statute lists.

allowed_only_for: position exempt under the Wage Order 4 executive exemption
other categories enumerated in Labor Code 1024.5 (not read)

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Labor Code section 1024.5 prohibits use of a consumer credit report for employment purposes unless the position of the person for whom the report is sought is exempt under the executive exemption as set forth in Wage Order 4 or meets one of the other enumerated categories contained in the statute.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.

rules.title: No retaliation when a worker updates their name, SSN or work authorization
rules.plain_english: You cannot punish a worker for updating their personal records after a lawful change of name, Social Security number or federal work authorization document.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: An employer may not discharge an employee or in any manner discriminate, retaliate, or take any adverse action against an employee because the employee updates or attempts to update his or her personal information based on a lawful change of name, social security number, or federal employment authorization document.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited page (17-8) is dated April 2021. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. The notes were edited: p. 17-8 is dated April 2021.

rules.title: Misusing E-Verify: civil penalty up to $10,000 per unlawful use
rules.plain_english: Use E-Verify only when federal law requires or allows it, and only after a job offer. Each violation can cost up to $10,000. Give the worker any federal tentative non-confirmation notice you receive about them.

parameters.lawful_timing: after an offer of employment, or as required by federal law, authorized by a federal agency, or as a condition of receiving federal funds
parameters.must_furnish_to_employee: any notification issued by a federal agency of a tentative non-confirmation (DLSE June 2026 list); the December 2020 manual words this as any SSA or DHS no-match notification specific to the employee's E-Verify case

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code sections 2814 and 1019.1-1019.4, manual pages 17-8 and 17-12); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm (2814, 1019.1 and 1019.2 entries, page dated June 2026)
rules.quote: In addition to other remedies that might be available, each unlawful use of the E-Verify system carries a civil penalty not to exceed $10,000.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages are dated April 2021 (17-8) and December 2020 (17-12). The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. For 1019.1-1019.4 the manual says: 'In addition to other remedies that might be available, a penalty of up to $10,000 may be awarded for each violation.' This adds penalty amounts to the existing rule unfair-immigration-related-practices.
rules.correction: must_furnish_to_employee and plain_english updated to DIR's newer June 2026 description of Labor Code 2814: give the employee any federal-agency notification of a tentative non-confirmation. The December 2020 manual's 'SSA or DHS no-match' wording is kept for reference. Added the 1019.2 reverification penalty ($10,000 per violation) from the same list. source_location and the notes' page dates updated. The $10,000 amounts are confirmed by both sources.

rules.title: No policies controlling workers' political activity
rules.plain_english: You cannot have rules that stop workers from taking part in politics or running for office, and you cannot threaten their jobs to influence how they act politically. Job applicants are covered too.

prohibited: rule or policy forbidding or controlling employees' political activities or affiliations
coercing or influencing political action by threat of discharge

rules.applies_to: Private California employers
rules.citation: Labor Code 1101, 1102; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4 and §§26.6-26.6.2
rules.quote: An employer may not make, adopt, or enforce any rule, regulation or policy that forbids, controls, directs or tends to direct the political activities or affiliations of employees.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages are dated December 2017 (17-10), August 2017 (26-2) and December 2020 (26-3). The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. §26.6.1: these sections do not apply to public entity employees.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. The notes' page dates were made exact (p. 26-2 is dated August 2017).

rules.title: No blacklisting: give only truthful statements about a former worker, and only on specific request
rules.plain_english: You cannot try to stop a former worker from getting hired elsewhere. Giving a truthful reason for termination is allowed when someone specifically asks about that person. Untruthful statements can cost triple damages.

parameters.prohibited: preventing re-employment of a former employee by misrepresentation
parameters.allowed: truthful statement of reasons for termination upon special (specific) request
parameters.damages: treble damages for untruthful statements (Labor Code 1054)
prima_facie_evidence: special mark or signal in references
information given without a special request

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: It is not illegal, however, for an employer to furnish, upon special request (i.e., a specific request for information regarding that employee), a truthful statement concerning the reasons for termination. (Labor Code § 1053)
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited page (26-2) is dated August 2017. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. §26.5: 'An employee who is damaged by an employer’s untruthful statements may recover treble damages. (Labor Code § 1054)'.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. The notes were edited: manual p. 26-2 is dated August 2017, not December 2020.

rules.title: Retaliation complaints: generally 1 year to file with the Labor Commissioner
rules.plain_english: A worker generally has one year after a firing, demotion or other retaliation to file with the Labor Commissioner. A federal OSHA complaint must be filed within 30 days. If the state dismisses a safety-retaliation complaint, the worker has 15 days to appeal. In those safety cases, an employer found in violation has 30 days to comply.

parameters.no_exhaustion_requirement: employee may sue directly in court (Labor Code 98.7(g), 244)

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_Retaliation.htm (FAQ answers on filing time limits and appeals); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.2 p. 17-1 and §17.1.4 p. 17-2); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm (introduction: 'within one year of the retaliatory act, unless stated otherwise')
rules.quote: The majority of the Labor Code Statutes and IWC Orders allow one year from the occurrence of the adverse action to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated May 2021. The same FAQ says: 'Employees must, however, file with federal OSHA within thirty days of the adverse action occurring', 'The Complainant ... must file their appeal within 15 days from the date of the receipt of the Determination', and 'the Respondent has 30 days to comply with the order.' It also gives two years for Labor Code 1197.5 complaints. That figure is out of date: the August 2026 Equal Pay Act FAQ requires EPA retaliation claims within one year, and wage-recovery limits changed under SB 642 (see the existing rule equal-pay-act-3-year-sol-6-year-lookback). The no-exhaustion rule is from DLSE Manual §17.1.4.
rules.correction: Scope of the 30-day compliance figure narrowed. In the FAQ, 'the Respondent has 30 days to comply with the order' comes in the answer on Labor Code 6310/6311 safety-retaliation appeals, so the key was renamed employer_days_to_comply_after_violation_finding_6310_6311 and plain_english limited to those cases. source_location now also names the manual (the no-exhaustion rule) and DIR's June 2026 list (the one-year rule). The 1-year, 30-day, 15-day and 90-day values are confirmed.

rules.title: Retaliating against a worker for asserting Labor Code rights: up to $10,000 per violation
rules.plain_english: Punishing a worker for complaining about unpaid wages, filing a claim, or using any Labor Code right can cost up to $10,000 per violation, paid to the worker, on top of back pay and reinstatement.

protected: filing or threatening a claim with the Labor Commissioner
oral or written complaint about unpaid wages
exercising any Labor Code or IWC order right
family member of a person who engaged in protected conduct

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 98.6; DLSE Enforcement Manual §17.1.4; DLSE Retaliation FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf (§17.1.4, Labor Code section 98.6, manual pages 17-1 to 17-2); https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_Retaliation.htm
rules.quote: In addition to other remedies that might be available, a civil penalty of up to $10,000 may be awarded to an employee for each violation of Labor Code section 98.6.
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2020. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. The remedies list is from the DLSE Retaliation FAQ ('make whole' remedy).

rules.title: Whistleblower retaliation: civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation plus attorney's fees
rules.plain_english: Retaliating against a worker who reports, or refuses to take part in, a suspected violation of law can cost a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation, paid to each employee who suffered it, plus the worker's attorney's fees.

protected: disclosing a suspected violation to a government or law enforcement agency, a supervisor or a person with authority to investigate
refusing to participate in a violation
family member of a person who engaged in protected conduct

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: In addition to other remedies that might be available, a civil penalty of up to $10,000 may be awarded for each violation and reasonable attorney’s fees may be awarded to a plaintiff who brings a successful action
rules.notes: Source is the DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual; the cited pages carry revision dates from December 2017. The current statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be read (bot protection), so a later amendment or renumbering cannot be ruled out. The whistleblower poster requirement is in the existing rule required-workplace-postings.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. DIR's June 2026 list confirms the $10,000 maximum and adds that it is awarded to each employee who suffered the violation. The attorney's-fee point rests on the December 2017 manual page. Rewording 2026-11-27: plain_english reworded to match this correction (DLSE list https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/HowToFileLinkCodeSections.htm re-read on 2026-11-27); no value changed.

rules.title: Pay transparency violations: $100 to $10,000 per violation
rules.plain_english: Leaving the pay range out of a job posting, refusing a pay-scale request, asking about salary history or not keeping wage-history records can cost $100 to $10,000 per violation.

parameters.enforcement: Labor Commissioner citation under Labor Code 98.74

rules.applies_to: California employers (job posting duty applies at 15+ employees)
rules.citation: Labor Code 432.3(d)(4); DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQ 'What are the remedies for a pay transparency law violation?')
rules.quote: An employer who violates the pay transparency law may be liable for civil penalties between $100 and $10,000 per violation.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026. This adds the penalty to the existing rule pay-scale-in-job-postings.

rules.title: Pay transparency complaints: 1 year from when the person learned of the violation
rules.plain_english: Someone harmed by a pay transparency violation can file with the Labor Commissioner within one year after learning of it, or sue in court.

parameters.clock_starts: date the person learned of the violation

rules.applies_to: California employers subject to Labor Code 432.3
rules.citation: Labor Code 432.3(d); DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQ 'Where and when can a person file a claim if they are aggrieved by a pay transparency law violation?')
rules.quote: A person who claims to be aggrieved by a pay transparency law violation may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner’s Office within one year after the date the person learned of the violation.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026.

rules.title: Give an employee their position's pay scale on request, and an applicant on reasonable request
rules.plain_english: If a current worker asks for the pay range for their job, you must give it. If a job applicant reasonably asks for the range of the job they applied for, you must give it too.

parameters.employee_request: pay scale for the employee's current position, upon request
parameters.applicant_request: pay scale for the position applied for, upon reasonable request
parameters.applicant_definition: person seeking employment who is not currently employed by the employer in any position

rules.applies_to: California employers
rules.citation: Labor Code 432.3(c)(1)-(2); DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQs 'Must an employer provide an employee the pay scale for their position?' and the applicant FAQ)
rules.quote: Yes, upon request, an employer must provide an employee the pay scale for their position.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026. The FAQ does not attach the 15-employee threshold to the on-request duties; it attaches it only to job postings.

rules.title: Do not ask applicants about salary history or rely on it
rules.plain_english: You cannot ask an applicant, yourself or through a recruiter, what they were paid before, and you cannot use it to decide whether to hire them or what to offer. You may ask what pay they expect. If they volunteer their history without being asked, you may consider it, but it never justifies a pay gap by sex, race or ethnicity.

parameters.may_not_seek: salary history including compensation and benefits (orally, in writing, personally or through an agent)
parameters.may_not_rely_on: salary history as a factor in offering employment or setting salary
allowed: consider salary history the applicant volunteers without prompting
parameters.exception: salary history disclosable to the public under state or federal law

rules.applies_to: California employers hiring applicants
rules.citation: Labor Code 432.3; DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQ 'Can an employer ask an applicant for employment about their salary history information?')
rules.quote: Generally, no, an employer cannot, orally or in writing, personally or through an agent, seek salary history information, including compensation and benefits, about an applicant for employment.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026.

rules.title: Keep job title and wage-rate history for each employee during employment plus 3 years
rules.plain_english: Keep each worker's job titles and pay rates for as long as they work for you plus three years. Keep wage-rate and job-classification records three years. The Labor Commissioner may inspect them.

retention.record: job title and wage rate history for each employee
names and addresses of all employees
hours worked daily, wages paid, piece-rate units and rates
wages and wage rates, job classifications and other terms and conditions of employment
personnel records on performance or grievances

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 226, 432.3(c)(4), 1174, 1197.5(e), 1198.5; DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQ 'How long must an employer keep Equal Pay Act-related records?')
rules.quote: Records "of a job title and wage rate history for each employee" (Id., at § 432.3, subd. (c)(4) [duration of employment plus 3 years])
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026. The existing rule pay-scale-in-job-postings gave this retention period from a secondary source; this rule states it from the DLSE page.

rules.title: Pay scale means a good-faith hourly or salary range, including piece-rate or commission ranges
rules.plain_english: The pay scale in a posting is your honest estimate of the hourly or salary range you expect to pay at hire. If the job pays by piece rate or commission, give that range too. Bonuses and benefits are optional.

parameters.pay_scale: good faith estimate of the salary or hourly wage range the employer reasonably expects to pay upon hire

rules.applies_to: California employers posting jobs (15+ employees)
rules.citation: Labor Code 432.3(m)(1); DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQs 'What does "pay scale" mean?' and 'Must the pay scale for a position include piece rate or commission wages?')
rules.quote: The "pay scale" for pay transparency law purposes means a good faith estimate of the salary or hourly wage range that an employer reasonably expects to pay for a position upon hire.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026.

rules.title: Recruiters and job boards must carry the pay scale; the 15-employee count needs at least one California employee
rules.plain_english: If a staffing agency, recruiter or job board posts your opening, give them the pay scale; they must include it. The Labor Commissioner applies the rule to any job that may be filled in California, in person or remotely. At least one of the 15 counted employees must be in California.

parameters.applies_to_positions: any position that may ever be filled in California, in person or remotely
parameters.third_party_posting: employer gives the pay scale to the third party; third party must include it

rules.applies_to: California employers with 15 or more employees, and third parties posting their jobs
rules.citation: Labor Code 432.3(c)(3), (c)(5); DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQs 'Must an employer include the pay scale for a position in any job posting?' and 'Who is counted as an employee...')
rules.quote: If such an employer engages a third party to announce, post, publish, or otherwise make known a job posting, it must provide the pay scale to the third party and the third party must include the pay scale in the job posting.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026. The count follows the method in the Labor Commissioner's 2022 COVID-19 Supplemental Paid Sick Leave FAQs, which were not read in this pass.

rules.title: Equal Pay Act: adverse action within 90 days of protected activity is presumed retaliatory
rules.plain_english: If you take action against a worker within 90 days after they asked about pay, discussed wages or complained about unequal pay, the law presumes it was retaliation. The worker has one year to file.

remedies: lost wages and work benefits with interest

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their employees, including construction contractors
rules.citation: Labor Code 1197.5(k), 98.6(b)(1); DLSE Equal Pay Act FAQ
rules.source: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/California_Equal_Pay_Act.htm (FAQs on retaliation for exercising Equal Pay Act rights)
rules.quote: There is a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if an employer engages in any action prohibited by the Equal Pay Act within 90 days of an employee engaging in protected activity specified in the statute.
rules.notes: FAQ page dated August 24, 2026: 'A claim must be filed no later than one year after the cause of action occurs.'

rules.title: ACA employer mandate applies at 50 or more full-time employees, counting FTEs, averaged over the prior year
rules.plain_english: You are an 'applicable large employer' for a year if last year you averaged at least 50 full-time employees, counting part-timers' hours as full-time equivalents. For 2026 the test uses your 2025 workforce; for 2027 it uses your 2026 workforce. Related companies under common control are counted together.

parameters.formula: floor(sum over 12 months of (full-time employees + FTEs, seasonal workers included) / 12) >= 50
parameters.rounding: round the average down to a whole number
parameters.aggregation: members of a controlled or affiliated service group under IRC 414(b), (c), (m), (o) counted together

rules.applies_to: All employers with workers in California (federal law)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-1 ¶(a)(4) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-1); https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-2 ¶(b)(1) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-2)
rules.quote: The term applicable large employer means, with respect to a calendar year, an employer that employed an average of at least 50 full-time employees (including full-time equivalent employees) on business days during the preceding calendar year.
rules.notes: The year mapping (2025 workforce for 2026 status) follows from 'preceding calendar year'. Aggregation is from the 54.4980H-2(d) examples, which refer to section 414(b), (c), (m), and (o).
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. Aggregation is stated directly in 54.4980H-1(a)(16) as well as in the 54.4980H-2(d) examples.

rules.title: Count FTEs as part-timers' monthly hours (max 120 each) divided by 120
rules.plain_english: To turn part-timers into full-time equivalents for each month, add their hours (counting no more than 120 per person) and divide by 120.

parameters.monthly_rounding: fractions counted; may round to nearest 0.01

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-2 ¶(c)(2) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-2)
rules.quote: The number of FTEs for each calendar month in the preceding calendar year is determined by calculating the aggregate number of hours of service for that calendar month for employees who were not full-time employees (but not more than 120 hours of service for any employee) and dividing that number by 120.
rules.notes: The regulation's example: 40 part-timers at 90 hours = 3,600 hours / 120 = 30 FTEs.

rules.title: Seasonal exception: over 50 for 120 days or less because of seasonal workers does not make you an ALE
rules.plain_english: If you went over 50 full-time employees and FTEs for 120 days or less last year, and the extra workers were seasonal, you are not an applicable large employer. Four calendar months may be counted as 120 days, and they do not have to be consecutive.
rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-2 ¶(b)(2) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-2)
rules.quote: If the sum of an employer's full-time employees and FTEs exceeds 50 for 120 days or less during the preceding calendar year, and the employees in excess of 50 who were employed during that period of no more than 120 days are seasonal workers, the employer is not considered to employ more than 50 full-time employees (including FTEs) and the employer is not an applicable large employer for the current calendar year.
rules.notes: 54.4980H-1(a)(39) lets employers use a reasonable, good-faith interpretation of 'seasonal worker'.

rules.title: A new business is an ALE in its first year if it expects and actually averages 50+
rules.plain_english: A company that did not exist last year is an applicable large employer this year if it reasonably expects to average 50 or more full-time employees and FTEs this year and actually does.

conditions: reasonably expected to average 50+ during current year
actually averages 50+ during current year
parameters.not_in_existence_means: not in existence on any business day of the prior calendar year

rules.applies_to: Employers not in existence during the preceding calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-2 ¶(b)(3) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-2)
rules.quote: An employer not in existence throughout the preceding calendar year is an applicable large employer for the current calendar year if the employer is reasonably expected to employ an average of at least 50 full-time employees (taking into account FTEs) on business days during the current calendar year and it actually employs an average of at least 50 full-time employees (taking into account FTEs) on business days during the calendar year.

rules.title: ACA full-time employee: 30 hours a week on average, or 130 hours in a month
rules.plain_english: For the ACA, a full-time employee averages at least 30 hours of service a week. A month with 130 or more hours counts as full-time. Under the optional weekly rule, the test is 120 hours in a four-week month or 150 hours in a five-week month.
rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-1 ¶(a)(21)(i)-(iii) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-1)
rules.quote: 130 hours of service in a calendar month is treated as the monthly equivalent of at least 30 hours of service per week, and this 130 hours of service monthly equivalency applies for both the look-back measurement method and the monthly measurement method for determining full-time employee status.
rules.notes: ¶(a)(21)(i): 'The term full-time employee means, with respect to a calendar month, an employee who is employed an average of at least 30 hours of service per week with an employer.'

rules.title: ACA hours of service include paid leave hours (vacation, holiday, sick, jury duty, layoff)
rules.plain_english: When counting ACA hours, include every hour paid for work and every hour paid while not working, such as vacation, holiday, illness, disability, layoff, jury duty, military duty or leave. Leave out bona fide volunteer hours and work-study hours.

includes: hours paid or entitled to payment for performance of duties
paid hours with no duties: vacation, holiday, illness, incapacity (including disability), layoff, jury duty, military duty, leave of absence
excludes: federal or similar work-study program hours
services with compensation from sources outside the United States
parameters.cross_member_rule: hours for one ALE member count for all members of the same ALE

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-1 ¶(a)(24) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-1)
rules.quote: The term hour of service means each hour for which an employee is paid, or entitled to payment, for the performance of duties for the employer; and each hour for which an employee is paid, or entitled to payment by the employer for a period of time during which no duties are performed due to vacation, holiday, illness, incapacity (including disability), layoff, jury duty, military duty or leave of absence (as defined in 29 CFR 2530.200b-2(a)).

rules.title: 4980H(a) penalty for not offering coverage: 1/12 of $2,000 (inflation-indexed) per full-time employee, minus 30
rules.plain_english: If you do not offer health coverage to at least 95% of full-time employees and their children, and even one full-time employee gets a subsidized Marketplace plan, you owe a monthly payment for all full-time employees after subtracting 30. The base is $2,000 a year per employee, adjusted for inflation.

parameters.reduction_allocation: 30 allocated ratably among ALE members by full-time count, each share rounded up
parameters.trigger: failure to offer minimum essential coverage (all but 5%, or 5 if greater) AND at least one full-time employee with a Section 1411 Certification (premium tax credit)
parameters.not_both: for a month a member owes 4980H(a) or 4980H(b), not both

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-1 ¶(a)(41) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-1); https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-4 ¶(a), (d), (e) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-4)
rules.quote: The term section 4980H(a) applicable payment amount means, with respect to any calendar month, 1/12 of $2,000, adjusted for inflation in accordance with section 4980H(c)(5) and any applicable guidance thereunder.
rules.notes: The 2026 and 2027 inflation-adjusted amounts are published by the IRS, and irs.gov and federalregister.gov are blocked here, so the dollar amounts are null and must be supplied before computing. The regulation's example uses the unindexed $2,000: 24 x $2,000 = $48,000.

rules.title: Offer coverage to all but 5% (or 5, if greater) of full-time employees, and to their dependents
rules.plain_english: To avoid the larger ACA penalty, offer health coverage every month to all but 5% of your full-time employees, or all but 5 if that is more. An offer counts only if it also covers the employee's children.

parameters.rule: not_offered <= max(5, 0.05 * full_time_employees)

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-4 ¶(a) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-4)
rules.quote: an applicable large employer member is treated as offering such coverage to its full-time employees (and their dependents) for a calendar month if, for that month, it offers such coverage to all but five percent (or, if greater, five) of its full-time employees (provided that an employee is treated as having been offered coverage only if the employer also offers coverage to that employee's dependents).

rules.title: 4980H(b) penalty for unaffordable or low-value coverage: 1/12 of $3,000 (indexed) per subsidized employee, capped
rules.plain_english: If you offer coverage but it is unaffordable or not minimum value, you owe a monthly payment for each full-time employee who gets a Marketplace subsidy. The base is $3,000 a year per employee, adjusted for inflation, and the total can never exceed what the no-offer penalty would have been.

parameters.counted_employees: full-time employees with a Section 1411 Certification, excluding those offered affordable minimum-value coverage under a safe harbor and those in a limited non-assessment period
parameters.cap: 4980H(a) amount for the month: (indexed $2,000 / 12) * (full-time employees - allocated share of 30)

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-1 ¶(a)(42) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-1); https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-5 ¶(a) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-5)
rules.quote: The term section 4980H(b) applicable payment amount means, with respect to any calendar month, 1/12 of $3,000, adjusted for inflation in accordance with section 4980H(c)(5) and any applicable guidance thereunder.
rules.notes: The 2026 and 2027 indexed amounts are not available because irs.gov is blocked.

rules.title: Affordability safe harbors: Form W-2, rate of pay (130 hours x hourly rate), or federal poverty line
rules.plain_english: Coverage is treated as affordable if the employee's cost for the cheapest self-only minimum-value plan stays under a set percentage of one of three measures: the employee's W-2 wages, 130 hours times their hourly rate, or the federal poverty line. The regulation says 9.5 percent. Check the IRS percentage for the plan year.

safe_harbors.form_w2: annual required contribution <= pct * Box 1 W-2 wages (prorated for partial-year offers)
safe_harbors.rate_of_pay_hourly: monthly contribution <= pct * 130 * min(hourly rate on first day of coverage period, lowest hourly rate in month)
safe_harbors.rate_of_pay_salaried: monthly contribution <= pct * monthly salary (not available if salary reduced)
safe_harbors.federal_poverty_line: monthly contribution <= pct * (single-person FPL for the state of employment / 12)

parameters.coverage_tested: lowest-cost self-only coverage providing minimum value
parameters.categories: may use different safe harbors for reasonable categories applied uniformly

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-5 ¶(e)(2)(i)-(iv) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-5)
rules.quote: An applicable large employer member satisfies the rate of pay safe harbor with respect to an hourly employee for a calendar month if the employee's required contribution for the calendar month for the applicable large employer member's lowest cost self-only coverage that provides minimum value does not exceed 9.5 percent of an amount equal to 130 hours multiplied by the lower of the employee's hourly rate of pay as of the first day of the coverage period (generally the first day of the plan year) or the employee's lowest hourly rate of pay during the calendar month.
rules.notes: The regulation text says 9.5 percent. Paragraph (e)(1) ties affordability to IRC 36B(c)(2)(C)(i), and 54.4980H-5(f) lets the IRS issue further guidance.
