This pass did not read any IRS-published percentage for 2026 or 2027 (irs.gov is blocked), so the plan-year percentages are null and should be confirmed before relying on 9.5.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. 9.5 percent is the regulatory text. The IRS-indexed plan-year percentages were not read (irs.gov blocked) and correctly remain null.

rules.title: First year as an ALE: offer coverage by April 1 to avoid January-March penalties
rules.plain_english: In the first year you become an applicable large employer, offering coverage by April 1 protects you from penalties for January through March for employees you had not covered the year before. The coverage must provide minimum value to avoid the 4980H(b) penalty for those months.

parameters.offer_deadline: April 1 of the first calendar year as an ALE
parameters.applies_to: employees not offered coverage at any point in the prior calendar year

rules.applies_to: Employers in their first year as an applicable large employer
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-2 ¶(b)(5) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-2)
rules.quote: if the applicable large employer offers coverage to the employee on or before April 1 of the first calendar year for which the employer is an applicable large employer, the employer will not be subject to an assessable payment under section 4980H by reason of its failure to offer coverage to the employee for January through March of that year
rules.notes: The relief applies only in the first year as an ALE. It does not come back if the employer drops below 50 and later becomes an ALE again.

rules.title: Missing even one day of coverage makes the whole month 'not offered'
rules.plain_english: If a full-time employee is not offered coverage for any day of a month, the whole month counts as not offered. There is no penalty for the month a new hire starts if they start after the 1st. The month an employee leaves counts as offered if coverage would have run the full month.

parameters.any_day_not_offered: entire month treated as not offered
parameters.start_month_if_start_date_not_first_of_m: no assessable payment for that employee for that month
parameters.termination_month: treated as offered if coverage would have been offered for the entire month

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-4 ¶(c) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-4)
rules.quote: If an applicable large employer member fails to offer coverage to a full-time employee for any day of a calendar month, that employee is treated as not offered coverage during that entire month, regardless of whether the employer uses the payroll period rule set forth in § 54.4980H-3(d)(1)(ii) or the weekly rule set forth in § 54.4980H-3(c)(3) to determine full-time employee status for the calendar month.

rules.title: Look-back method: 3-12 month measurement, stability of at least 6 months, administrative period up to 90 days
rules.plain_english: For variable-hour crews you may decide full-time status by looking back over a 3 to 12 month measurement period. Anyone who averaged 30 or more hours must be treated as full-time for a following stability period of at least 6 months, and no shorter than the measurement period. An optional setup period between them can last up to 90 days.

parameters.stability_period_if_full_time: at least 6 consecutive calendar months and not shorter than the measurement period
parameters.stability_period_if_not_full_time: not longer than the measurement period
parameters.new_hire_combined_limit: initial measurement period + administrative period may not extend beyond the last day of the first calendar month beginning on or after the first anniversary of the start date
parameters.uniformity: same rules for all employees in a permissible category

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-1 ¶(a)(46) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-1); https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-3 ¶(d)(1), (d)(3) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-3)
rules.quote: The term standard measurement period means a period of at least three but not more than 12 consecutive months that is used by an applicable large employer member as part of the look-back measurement method in § 54.4980H-3(d).
rules.notes: 54.4980H-3(d)(1)(iii): 'The stability period must be at least six consecutive calendar months but no shorter in duration than the standard measurement period.' (d)(1)(vi): 'The administrative period following the standard measurement period may last up to 90 days.'

rules.title: A rehired worker counts as a new employee only after 13 straight weeks with no hours
rules.plain_english: When a laid-off worker comes back, you may treat them as a new hire for ACA purposes only if they had no hours of service for at least 13 consecutive weeks. Otherwise they keep their prior status. Under the optional parity rule you may use a shorter break of at least 4 weeks if it is longer than their prior period of work.

parameters.parity_rule_option: break of at least 4 consecutive weeks that exceeds the employee's immediately preceding period of employment

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-3 ¶(c)(4)(i), (v) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-3)
rules.quote: may be treated as a new employee upon the resumption of services only if the employee did not have an hour of service for the applicable large employer for a period of at least 13 consecutive weeks immediately preceding the resumption of services.
rules.notes: This matters for construction crews laid off between projects and recalled.

rules.title: ACA 'dependents' are children under 26; spouses are not required
rules.plain_english: The required offer to dependents means the employee's children until the month they turn 26. Stepchildren and foster children are excluded, and spouses do not have to be offered coverage under this rule.

parameters.age_26_month: child is a dependent for the entire month in which they turn 26

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980H-1 ¶(a)(12) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980H-1)
rules.quote: The term dependent does not include the spouse of an employee.

rules.title: File Forms 1094-C/1095-C with the IRS by February 28 (paper) or March 31 (electronic)
rules.plain_english: Applicable large employers file Forms 1094-C and 1095-C with the IRS by February 28 on paper, or by March 31 if filed electronically. For tax year 2026, February 28, 2027 is a Sunday, so a paper filing is due Monday, March 1, 2027. The electronic deadline is Wednesday, March 31, 2027.

parameters.weekend_holiday_rule: next day that is not a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday (26 CFR 301.7503-1)

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (50+ full-time employees including FTEs in the prior calendar year), including California construction contractors
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-301.6056-1 ¶(c)(1), (e) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=301.6056-1); https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-301.7503-1 ¶(a) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=301.7503-1)
rules.quote: An applicable large employer member must file the return and transmittal form required under paragraph (d)(2) of this section on or before February 28 (March 31 if filed electronically) of the year succeeding the calendar year to which it relates in accordance with any applicable guidance and the instructions to the form.
rules.notes: The tax year 2026 dates come from applying 301.7503-1 to a calendar; February 28, 2027 is a Sunday. Most ALEs must file electronically because they file 10 or more information returns (see hr-aca-efile-10-return-threshold). The 2026 Form 1094-C/1095-C instructions on irs.gov were not read.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. The 2027-03-01 and 2027-03-31 dates are computed from the regulation and a calendar, as the rule says.

rules.title: Furnish Form 1095-C to full-time employees by January 31, with an automatic 30-day extension
rules.plain_english: Give each full-time employee a Form 1095-C by January 31 of the next year. The rules grant an automatic 30-day extension, which for tax year 2026 runs to Tuesday, March 2, 2027. Mail it to the employee's last known permanent address, or deliver it electronically only with the employee's consent.

parameters.mailing: first-class mail to last known permanent address (or temporary address) satisfies the requirement

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers (to each full-time employee)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-301.6056-1 ¶(g)(1)-(2), (m) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=301.6056-1)
rules.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this paragraph (g)(1), each statement required by this section for a calendar year must be furnished to a full-time employee on or before January 31 of the year succeeding the calendar year in accordance with applicable Internal Revenue Service procedures and instructions. Applicable large employers are granted an automatic, 30-day extension of time in which to furnish these statements.
rules.notes: Under ¶(m), the automatic extension in (g)(1) applies to calendar years beginning after December 31, 2021. March 2, 2027 is January 31, 2027 plus 30 days and is computed, not quoted. Any later change to section 6056 furnishing in the statute or IRS notices was not checked because uscode.house.gov and irs.gov are blocked.
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. 301.7503-1(a) counts authorized extensions in finding the last day, which supports computing the extended date from January 31. The computed date 2027-03-02 is not a weekend or holiday. It is still a computed date, as the parameter name says.

rules.title: E-file information returns, including 1095-C, if you file 10 or more of any kind in a year
rules.plain_english: If you must file 10 or more information returns in a calendar year, counting W-2s, 1099s and 1095-Cs together, all of them must be filed electronically.

parameters.hardship_waiver: may be requested from the IRS

rules.applies_to: Employers filing federal information returns (including ALEs filing Forms 1094-C/1095-C)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-301.6011-2 ¶(b)(1)-(2), (c)(1), (c)(4), (g) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=301.6011-2)
rules.quote: No person is required to file information returns electronically in a calendar year unless the person is required to file at least 10 returns during that calendar year.
rules.notes: Applies to information returns filed in calendar years beginning after December 31, 2023 (¶(g)).

rules.title: Electronic 1095-C delivery requires the employee's affirmative consent
rules.plain_english: You may send Form 1095-C electronically only if the employee has affirmatively agreed to receive it that way, in a manner that shows they can open it. Otherwise send it on paper.

parameters.consent_form: electronic, reasonably demonstrating access; or paper confirmed electronically
parameters.withdrawal: consent withdrawn before furnishing defeats electronic delivery

rules.applies_to: Applicable large employers furnishing Form 1095-C
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-301.6056-2 ¶(a)(1)-(2) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=301.6056-2)
rules.quote: The recipient must have affirmatively consented to receive the statement in an electronic format.

rules.title: Late or incorrect information returns (W-2, 1099, 1095-C): $250 per return before inflation adjustment
rules.plain_english: Each information return filed late or wrong can cost $250, or $50 if fixed within 30 days, or $100 if fixed by August 1. Annual caps apply, with lower caps for businesses with gross receipts of $5 million or less. These are base amounts that the IRS adjusts for inflation.
rules.applies_to: Employers filing W-2, 1099, 1094-C/1095-C and other information returns
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-301.6721-1 ¶(a)(1), (b)(1)-(2), (f)(1), (i) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=301.6721-1)
rules.quote: A penalty of $250 is imposed for each information return (as defined in section 6724(d)(1) and paragraph (h) of this section) with respect to which a failure (as defined in section 6721(a)(2) and paragraph (a)(2) of this section) occurs.
rules.notes: ¶(i) requires inflation adjustment of these dollar amounts under section 6721(f). The IRS-published 2026 and 2027 amounts were not read (irs.gov is blocked). Intentional disregard carries higher penalties under ¶(g).
rules.correction: No parameter, citation or scope change. Every base amount matches: $250/$3,000,000; $50/$500,000; $100/$1,500,000; small-business test $5,000,000 with caps $1,000,000/$175,000/$500,000. The inflation-adjusted amounts correctly remain null.

rules.title: Late or incorrect employee statements (W-2, 1095-C): $250 per statement before inflation adjustment
rules.plain_english: Each employee copy (W-2, 1095-C and similar) furnished late or wrong can cost $250 before inflation adjustment, with a $3,000,000 annual cap. Intentional disregard costs more.
rules.applies_to: Employers furnishing W-2, 1095-C and other payee statements
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-301.6722-1 ¶(a)(1), (f) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=301.6722-1)
rules.quote: A penalty of $250 is imposed for each payee statement (as defined in section 6724(d)(2) and paragraph (e)(2) of this section) with respect to which a failure (as defined in section 6722(a) and paragraph (a)(2) of this section) occurs.
rules.notes: The section applies to payee statements due on or after January 1, 2024. The inflation-adjusted amounts were not read.

rules.title: Group health plan coverage must start within 90 days of eligibility
rules.plain_english: If you offer a group health plan, coverage for an eligible employee must be able to begin no later than 90 days after they become eligible. A bona fide orientation period may not exceed one month.

parameters.orientation_period_max: one month (add one calendar month, subtract one day, from the start date)

rules.applies_to: Employers sponsoring group health plans (and their insurers)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.9815-2708 ¶(a), (c)(3)(iii) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.9815-2708)
rules.quote: A group health plan, and a health insurance issuer offering group health insurance coverage, must not apply any waiting period that exceeds 90 days, in accordance with the rules of this section.
rules.notes: ¶(c)(3)(iii): 'an orientation period is permitted only if it does not exceed one month.' The parallel DOL and HHS regulations were not read.

rules.title: Federal COBRA applies once you normally employ 20 or more employees
rules.plain_english: Your group health plan is exempt from federal COBRA if last year you had fewer than 20 employees on at least half of your typical business days. Part-timers count as fractions, while owners, independent contractors and directors are not counted.

parameters.test: fewer than 20 employees on at least 50% of typical business days in the preceding calendar year
parameters.part_time_counting: fraction = hours worked / hours required to be full-time (daily or pay-period basis, applied consistently for the year)
parameters.controlled_group: employees of the controlled group counted together

rules.applies_to: Employers sponsoring group health plans
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980B-2 Q&A-5(a)-(e) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980B-2)
rules.quote: An employer is considered to have normally employed fewer than 20 employees during a particular calendar year if, and only if, it had fewer than 20 employees on at least 50 percent of its typical business days during that year.
rules.notes: Smaller California employers may be covered by Cal-COBRA instead. Its rules (Insurance Code and Health and Safety Code, DMHC and CDI pages) could not be read.

rules.title: A COBRA qualifying event must cause a loss of plan coverage; quits, layoffs, strikes and lockouts count
rules.plain_english: An event (death, termination other than for gross misconduct, reduction of hours, divorce or legal separation, Medicare entitlement, a child losing dependent status, or a retiree-employer bankruptcy) is a COBRA qualifying event only if it makes the employee, spouse or child lose coverage under the plan's terms. It does not matter whether the worker quit or was let go; a layoff, strike or lockout that ends coverage is a qualifying event.

events: termination (other than for gross misconduct) or reduction of hours
covered employee becomes entitled to Medicare
dependent child ceases to be a dependent under the plan
bankruptcy of the employer a covered employee retired from
parameters.lose_coverage_means: cease to be covered under the same terms and conditions as immediately before the event
parameters.strike_or_lockout: a termination or reduction of hours (qualifying event if it causes a loss of coverage)
parameters.layoff: qualifying event if it causes a loss of coverage
parameters.medicare_entitlement_means: enrolled in Part A or Part B (eligibility alone is not entitlement)

rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980B-4 Q&A-1(b)-(c) and Q&A-2 (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-24: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-24/title-26.xml?section=54.4980B-4)
rules.quote: An event satisfies this paragraph (c) if, under the terms of the group health plan, the event causes the covered employee, or the spouse or a dependent child of the covered employee, to lose coverage under the plan.
rules.notes: Q&A-2: 'Thus, it does not matter whether the employee voluntarily terminated or was discharged.' 'For example, a strike or a lockout is a termination or reduction of hours that constitutes a qualifying event if the strike or lockout results in a loss of coverage' as described in paragraph (c) of Q&A-1. Similarly, a layoff that results in such a loss of coverage is a qualifying event. The Medicare wording is from 54.4980B-7 Q&A-3 (entitled on the effective date of enrollment in Part A or B; 'merely being eligible to enroll in Medicare does not constitute being entitled to Medicare benefits').

rules.title: Notify the plan administrator of a COBRA qualifying event within 30 days
rules.plain_english: When an employee covered by the health plan is terminated, has hours cut, dies or becomes entitled to Medicare, notify the plan administrator within 30 days.

parameters.clock_starts: date of the qualifying event (or date coverage is lost, if the plan measures from loss of coverage)
employer_reported_events: termination of employment (other than gross misconduct)
parameters.notice_contents: enough to identify the plan, covered employee, qualifying event and its date

rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-2590.606-2 ¶(a)-(c) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=2590.606-2)
rules.quote: In all other cases, not later than 30 days after the date on which the qualifying event occurred.

rules.title: COBRA election notice: 14 days after the administrator is notified, or 44 days if the employer is the administrator
rules.plain_english: The plan administrator must send the COBRA election notice within 14 days of learning of the qualifying event. If you, the employer, are also the plan administrator, you have 44 days from the event or the loss of coverage.

parameters.employer_is_administrator_clock_starts: qualifying event date (or loss of coverage date if the plan so provides)

rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-2590.606-4 ¶(b)(1)-(2) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=2590.606-4)
rules.quote: Except as provided in paragraph (b)(2) or (3) of this section, upon receipt of a notice of qualifying event furnished in accordance with § 2590.606-2 or § 2590.606-3, the administrator shall furnish to each qualified beneficiary, not later than 14 days after receipt of the notice of qualifying event, a notice meeting the requirements of paragraph (b)(4) of this section.

rules.title: COBRA general rights notice: within 90 days after plan coverage begins
rules.plain_english: Give each newly covered employee and spouse a written COBRA general notice within 90 days after their health coverage starts.

parameters.earlier_if: an election notice is due sooner (2590.606-4(b))

rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-2590.606-1 ¶(b)(1) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=2590.606-1)
rules.quote: The date that is 90 days after the date on which such individual's coverage under the plan commences, or, if later, the date that is 90 days after the date on which the plan first becomes subject to the continuation coverage requirements; or

rules.title: COBRA election window: at least 60 days
rules.plain_english: A former employee or family member gets at least 60 days to elect COBRA, counted from the later of the date coverage would end or the date the election notice is provided. For a divorce, legal separation or a child no longer counting as a dependent, the employee or a family member must tell the plan administrator within 60 days after the later of the event or the date coverage would end; if the plan is not told in time, it does not have to offer COBRA.

parameters.clock_starts: later of loss of coverage date or date election notice is provided
parameters.beneficiary_notice_clock: later of the qualifying event date or the date the qualified beneficiary would lose coverage
beneficiary_notice_events: dependent child ceasing to be a dependent under the plan

rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980B-6 Q&A-1(a), Q&A-2(a) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980B-6)
rules.quote: The election period must not end before the date that is 60 days after the later of
rules.notes: Q&A-2(a) of the same section: the covered employee or qualified beneficiary must notify the plan administrator of a divorce, legal separation or a child's loss of dependent status; 'The group health plan is not required to offer the qualified beneficiary an opportunity to elect COBRA continuation coverage if the notice is not provided to the plan administrator within 60 days after the later of' (1) the date of the qualifying event or (2) the date the qualified beneficiary would lose coverage.
rules.correction: Adversarial review 2026-11-25 (sources re-fetched that day): added the beneficiary's 60-day notice duty for divorce, legal separation and loss of dependent status (Q&A-2(a)), which the tool had reported as not in the rulebook. The 60-day election rule is unchanged. Rewording 2026-11-27: plain_english reworded to match this correction (26 CFR 54.4980B-6 Q&A-2 re-read in the eCFR versioner API, title 26 issue 2026-11-18 on 2026-11-27); no value changed.

rules.title: COBRA lasts 18 months after termination or hours cut (29 with disability, 36 for other events)
rules.plain_english: COBRA after a termination or reduction in hours lasts up to 18 months, or 29 months with a disability extension. The extension applies only if Social Security finds the worker or a covered family member disabled at some time in the first 60 days of COBRA coverage, and the plan administrator is told within 60 days after that finding and before the 18 months end. A second qualifying event, such as death or divorce, during that time can extend it to 36 months. The months count from the qualifying event, or from the loss of coverage only if the plan says so.

parameters.measured_from: date of qualifying event (or loss of coverage if plan so provides)
disability_extension_requires: qualifying event is a termination or reduction of hours
a qualified beneficiary is determined by the Social Security Administration (title II or XVI) to have been disabled at any time during the first 60 days of COBRA coverage
a qualified beneficiary notifies the plan administrator within 60 days after the determination is issued and before the original 18 months end

rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980B-7 Q&A-4(a)-(c), Q&A-6(b) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980B-7)
rules.quote: In the case of a qualifying event that is a termination of employment or reduction of hours of employment, the maximum coverage period ends 18 months after the qualifying event if there is no disability extension, and 29 months after the qualifying event if there is a disability extension.
rules.notes: Q&A-5(c)-(d): disabled 'to have been disabled at any time during the first 60 days of COBRA continuation coverage.' and notice 'provides notice to the plan administrator of the disability determination on a date that is both within 60 days after the date the determination is issued and before the end of the original 18-month maximum coverage period that applies to the qualifying event.' Q&A-4(b)(1): 'The end of the maximum coverage period is measured from the date of the qualifying event even if the qualifying event does not result in a loss of coverage under the plan until a later date.' Measuring from the loss of coverage is allowed only if the plan provides for it (both the 30-day employer notice and the maximum period run from the loss).
rules.correction: Adversarial review 2026-11-25 (sources re-fetched that day): added disability_extension_requires (Q&A-5(b)-(d)) and loss_of_coverage_measurement_requires_plan_terms (Q&A-4(b)). The 18/29/36-month values are unchanged. Rewording 2026-11-27: plain_english reworded to match this correction (26 CFR 54.4980B-7 Q&A-4 and Q&A-5 re-read in the eCFR versioner API, title 26 issue 2026-11-18 on 2026-11-27); no value changed.

rules.title: COBRA premium may not exceed 102% of the plan cost (150% during a disability extension)
rules.plain_english: You may charge COBRA participants up to 102% of the plan's cost, or up to 150% during months 19 to 29 of a disability extension, but only for coverage that includes the disabled person.

parameters.disability_150_percent_only_if: the coverage covers the disabled qualified beneficiary and would not be required without the disability extension

rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year

rules.quote: For any period of COBRA continuation coverage, a group health plan can require the payment of an amount that does not exceed 102 percent of the applicable premium for that period.
rules.notes: Q&A-1(b): 'A group health plan is permitted to require the payment of an amount that does not exceed 150 percent of the applicable premium for any period of COBRA continuation coverage covering a disabled qualified beneficiary' (for example, whether single or family coverage) if the coverage would not be required to be made available in the absence of a disability extension.
rules.correction: Adversarial review 2026-11-25 (sources re-fetched that day): added disability_150_percent_only_if from Q&A-1(b); 102% and 150% are unchanged. rules.title: COBRA payments: 30-day grace period; first payment not due before 45 days after election
rules.plain_english: Each COBRA payment is on time if paid within 30 days after the start of the coverage period. The first payment cannot be required earlier than 45 days after the person elects COBRA.
rules.applies_to: Employers with group health plans that normally employed 20 or more employees in the prior calendar year
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-54.4980B-8 Q&A-5(a)-(b) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-26.xml?section=54.4980B-8)
rules.quote: Except as provided in this paragraph (a) or in paragraph (b) or (d) of this Q&A-5, timely payment for a period of COBRA continuation coverage under a group health plan means payment that is made to the plan by the date that is 30 days after the first day of that period.
rules.notes: Q&A-5(b): 'a plan cannot require payment for any period of COBRA continuation coverage for a qualified beneficiary earlier than 45 days after the date on which the election of COBRA continuation coverage is made for that qualified beneficiary.'

rules.title: Federal FMLA covers employers with 50+ employees in 20+ workweeks this year or last
rules.plain_english: The federal Family and Medical Leave Act applies to you if you had 50 or more employees on each working day of at least 20 calendar weeks in this year or last year.

integrated_employer_test: degree of common ownership or financial control

rules.applies_to: Private employers (federal law)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-825.104 ¶(a), (c) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=825.104)
rules.quote: An employer covered by FMLA is any person engaged in commerce or in any industry or activity affecting commerce, who employs 50 or more employees for each working day during each of 20 or more calendar workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year.
rules.notes: The California Family Rights Act (CFRA) has its own, different coverage rules. CRD pages and Gov. Code 12945.2 could not be read, so CFRA is not encoded here.

rules.title: FMLA eligibility: 12 months of employment, 1,250 hours in the past year, 50 employees within 75 miles
rules.plain_english: A worker can take FMLA leave once they have worked for you at least 12 months (not necessarily in a row), worked at least 1,250 hours in the 12 months before the leave, and work at a site where you have 50 or more employees within 75 miles.

parameters.break_in_service_years_disregard: employment before a break of 7 years or more need not be counted (with USERRA and written-agreement exceptions)

rules.applies_to: Private employers with 50 or more employees in 20 or more workweeks (federal FMLA)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-825.110 ¶(a)-(b) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=825.110)
rules.quote: Has been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave

rules.title: FMLA 50-in-75-miles test for construction workers uses their home base or reporting site
rules.plain_english: Construction workers have no fixed worksite, so the 50-employees-within-75-miles test uses the place they are assigned to as home base, get assignments from, or report to. A jobsite trailer office can be the worksite for workers hired locally. Measure the 75 miles by road.

parameters.no_fixed_worksite_rule: worksite = site assigned as home base, from which work is assigned, or to which they report
parameters.jobsite_trailer_example: locally hired workers who report daily to an on-site trailer office: the construction site is their worksite; staff sent from headquarters keep headquarters as worksite
parameters.distance_measure: surface miles over public roads by the shortest route

rules.applies_to: Private employers with 50 or more employees in 20 or more workweeks (federal FMLA)

rules.quote: For employees with no fixed worksite, e.g., construction workers, transportation workers (e.g., truck drivers, seamen, pilots), salespersons, etc., the worksite is the site to which they are assigned as their home base, from which their work is assigned, or to which they report.

rules.title: FMLA leave: up to 12 workweeks in a 12-month period
rules.plain_english: An eligible worker may take up to 12 workweeks of job-protected leave in a 12-month period for a new child, a serious health condition of their own or of a family member, or a qualifying military exigency.

parameters.period: 12-month period chosen by employer (calendar year, fixed year, forward or rolling backward)
reasons: care for spouse, child or parent with serious health condition

rules.applies_to: Private employers with 50 or more employees in 20 or more workweeks (federal FMLA)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-825.200 ¶(a)-(b) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=825.200)
rules.quote: Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons:

rules.title: FMLA military caregiver leave: up to 26 workweeks in a single 12-month period
rules.plain_english: To care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible worker may take up to 26 workweeks in a single 12-month period that starts with the first day of that leave. All FMLA leave combined in that period is capped at 26 weeks.

parameters.period: single 12-month period measured forward from first day of caregiver leave

rules.applies_to: Private employers with 50 or more employees in 20 or more workweeks (federal FMLA)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-825.200 ¶(f)-(g) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=825.200)
rules.quote: An eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 26 workweeks of leave during a single 12-month period to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness.

rules.title: FMLA notices: eligibility, rights and designation notices within 5 business days
rules.plain_english: When a worker asks for leave, or you learn that leave may qualify, tell them within 5 business days whether they are eligible. Once you have enough information, tell them within 5 business days whether the leave is designated as FMLA.

parameters.trigger: employee requests leave or employer learns leave may be FMLA-qualifying

rules.applies_to: Private employers with 50 or more employees in 20 or more workweeks (federal FMLA)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-825.300 ¶(b)(1), (c), (d)(1) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=825.300)
rules.quote: When an employee requests FMLA leave, or when the employer acquires knowledge that an employee's leave may be for an FMLA-qualifying reason, the employer must notify the employee of the employee's eligibility to take FMLA leave within five business days, absent extenuating circumstances.

rules.title: FMLA poster: required even with no eligible employees; willful failure up to $216 per offense
rules.plain_english: Every FMLA-covered employer must display the FMLA poster where employees and applicants can see it, even if no one is eligible yet. Electronic posting is allowed. A willful failure can cost up to $216 per offense.

parameters.general_notice_distribution_if_any_eligi: include in employee handbooks or other written benefit/leave guidance if they exist, otherwise give a copy to each new employee upon hiring (825.300(a)(3))

rules.applies_to: Private employers with 50 or more employees in 20 or more workweeks (federal FMLA)
rules.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-825.300 ¶(a)(1)-(2) (text read 2026-11-25 through the eCFR versioner API, version as of 2026-11-20: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-20/title-29.xml?section=825.300)

rules.notes: $216 is the amount in the eCFR text of 2026-11-20. DOL adjusts it for inflation. The poster (WH 1420) is listed in the existing rule required-workplace-postings.

rules.title: City of San Diego minimum wage: $17.75/hour (2026)
rules.plain_english: For hours worked inside San Diego city limits in 2026, pay at least $17.75 an hour. The rate covers any employee who works at least 2 hours inside the city in one or more calendar weeks of the year, including crews from out-of-town companies, for every hour they work inside the city. Small businesses are not exempt, and tips do not count toward the minimum. It does not apply to work inside a federal enclave such as a military base, where the City ordinance does not reach.

parameters.ordinance: San Diego Municipal Code Ch. 3, Art. 9, Div. 1
not_covered: work performed within a federal enclave (e.g., a military base)
persons not entitled to the California minimum wage
parameters.coverage_test: employee performs at least 2 hours of work within the City in one or more calendar weeks of the year (OLSE FAQ 7); then every hour worked within the City is owed the City rate
parameters.communities_source: OLSE 'City of San Diego Communities by Council District' https://www.sandiego.gov/sites/default/files/tr_communities_by_council_district.pdf; confirm a specific address on the OLSE interactive geographic boundaries map

rules.applies_to: Employers of any size, for employees entitled to the California minimum wage who work at least 2 hours within the City of San Diego in one or more calendar weeks of the year. The Ordinance does not cover work inside a federal enclave such as a military base, public-agency employees, or independent contractors (OLSE FAQs 7, 8, 23, 24)
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 3, Article 9, Division 1 (Earned Sick Leave and Minimum Wage Ordinance)
rules.source: https://www.sandiego.gov/sites/default/files/mwo-faqs.pdf (FAQ 3, updated January 2026); https://www.sandiego.gov/olse/minimum-wage/earned-sick-leave (Minimum Wage table); https://www.sandiego.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/minimum-wage-rates_historical_09.2026.pdf; communities list: https://www.sandiego.gov/sites/default/files/tr_communities_by_council_district.pdf
rules.quote: As of January 1, 2026, the minimum wage is $17.75 per hour.
rules.notes: Coverage per the OLSE page: 'It is applicable to employees who perform at least two (2) hours of work in one or more calendar weeks of the year within the geographic boundaries of San Diego.' The rate history is from the OLSE historical rates PDF (September 2026). Coverage (OLSE FAQ 7, January 2026): 'Employees who perform at least two hours of work within the geographic boundaries of the City in one or more calendar weeks of the year and who are entitled to be paid minimum wage under California law are entitled to the benefits of the Ordinance.' The OLSE page says the same: 'It is applicable to employees who perform at least two (2) hours of work in one or more calendar weeks of the year within the geographic boundaries of San Diego.' The 2027 notice words it as 'two (2) or more hours in any work week'. None of these makes coverage a week-by-week test, and the ordinance text (docs.sandiego.gov) could not be fetched, so a tool must not drop the City rate just because this week's in-city hours are under 2.
rules.correction: applies_to narrowed to match OLSE FAQs 7, 8, 23 and 24 (mwo-faqs.pdf, January 2026). The Ordinance covers only employees entitled to the California minimum wage (so exempt salaried staff are outside it). It does not apply to work inside a federal enclave such as a military base, which matters for San Diego construction, or to public-agency employees, and it excludes independent contractors. Added not_covered to the parameters and a federal-enclave sentence to plain_english. $17.75 (2026-01-01), the 2-hour coverage test, no small-business exemption, no tip credit and the whole rate history (10.50 to 18.35) are confirmed. Adversarial review 2026-11-25 (sources re-fetched that day): the coverage test was stated as '2 or more hours in a week', which a tool read as a weekly on/off switch. OLSE FAQ 7 and the OLSE page say 'at least two hours ... in one or more calendar weeks of the year'. Added coverage_test and coverage_is_not_a_per_week_test; plain_english and applies_to reworded. The 2-hour figure and all rates are unchanged. Added communities_within_city_by_council_district from the OLSE communities PDF (geography only; a work address still needs the OLSE boundaries map).

rules.title: City of San Diego minimum wage: $18.35/hour from January 1, 2027

not_covered: work performed within a federal enclave (e.g., a military base)
persons not entitled to the California minimum wage

rules.title: San Diego earned sick leave: 1 hour per 30 hours worked in the city; 80-hour accrual cap; 40-hour use cap
rules.plain_english: Workers earn at least 1 hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked inside San Diego city limits, and unused hours carry over. You may cap total accrual at 80 hours and yearly use at 40 hours, or front-load 40 hours at the start of each benefit year instead.

parameters.pay_rate_when_used: employee's regular rate at time of use
parameters.state_law_preemption_guidance: follow state law where more generous (e.g., reinstate balance if rehired within 1 year; payment by next regular payday)

rules.applies_to: Employers of any size, for employees entitled to the California minimum wage who work at least 2 hours within the City of San Diego in one or more calendar weeks of the year. The Ordinance does not cover work inside a federal enclave such as a military base, public-agency employees, or independent contractors (OLSE FAQs 7, 8, 23, 24)

rules.quote: Employees must accrue no less than one (1) hour of earned sick leave for every thirty (30) hours worked within the geographic boundaries of the City; employers may cap the total accrual of sick leave at eighty (80) hours.
rules.notes: The OLSE page also says: 'Employers may satisfy the accrual and carry-over requirements if no less than forty (40) hours of earned sick leave are awarded to an employee at the beginning of each benefit year. Employers may limit an employee's use of earned sick leave to forty (40) hours in a benefit year.' FAQ 18 says front-loaded hours may not be prorated. The OLSE SB 616 notice tells employers to follow the more generous state rules. The state paid sick leave rules are in the existing paid-sick-leave-* rules.
rules.correction: applies_to narrowed to match OLSE FAQs 7, 8, 23 and 24 (mwo-faqs.pdf, January 2026). The Ordinance covers only employees entitled to the California minimum wage (so exempt salaried staff are outside it). It does not apply to work inside a federal enclave such as a military base, which matters for San Diego construction, or to public-agency employees, and it excludes independent contractors. 1 hour per 30, 80-hour accrual cap, 40-hour use cap, 40-hour front-load with no proration, carryover, day-one accrual, regular-rate pay and the SB 616 guidance are all confirmed. Adversarial review 2026-11-25 (sources re-fetched that day): applies_to reworded to the OLSE FAQ 7 coverage test ('in one or more calendar weeks of the year'); no value changed.

rules.title: San Diego sick leave may be used as 'safe time' for domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking
rules.plain_english: Workers may use San Diego sick leave for themselves or a family member to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, for example medical care, counseling, relocation or legal proceedings.

safe_time_purposes: medical attention for injury caused by domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking

rules.title: San Diego traffic control (flagger) wage under City permits: $76.87/hour total ($49.20 base + $27.67 benefits)
rules.plain_english: Flaggers and other traffic control workers on a City of San Diego traffic control permit must be paid at least the County prevailing wage for Laborer Group 1. For permits issued from October 9, 2026 to June 30, 2027 that is $49.20 base plus $27.67 in benefits per hour ($76.87), $101.47 for overtime and Saturdays, and $126.07 for Sundays and holidays. The rate in effect when the permit is issued, including its predetermined increase, applies for the life of the permit: from July 1, 2027 those permits owe $3.66 more per hour ($80.53 total), split between wages and benefits, and no further adjustments. Benefits not paid into plans must be paid as cash.

parameters.rate_locked_at: date the City issues the traffic control permit, for the permit's duration
parameters.basis: DIR prevailing wage, Laborer: Building Construction Group 1, San Diego County
parameters.rate_updates: rates follow the DIR Laborer Group 1 determination: new DIR rates take effect 10 days after issue, typically issued each February and August; a permit issued later may carry a different rate

rules.applies_to: Employers performing traffic control work under a City of San Diego traffic control permit (SDMC 129.0742)
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 3, Article 10, Division 1 (Traffic Control Worker Minimum Wage Ordinance), as amended by O-21876
rules.quote: The applicable wage rate, including any predetermined increase, is determined as of the date the City issues a traffic control permit and remains in effect for the duration of the permit.
rules.notes: The rates come from the OLSE page and the November 2026 notice. The holiday list on the OLSE page includes Labor Day, but the historical-rates PDF omits it; the parameters follow the OLSE page. The notice says: 'Effective July 1, 2027, there will be an increase of $3.66 to be allocated to wages and/or fringes.' The ordinance took effect October 18, 2023. Notice (Rev. 11/3/26): 'Effective July 1, 2027, there will be an increase of $3.66 to be allocated to wages and/or fringes. No further wage adjustments will apply to permits issued during this timeframe.' Historical-rates PDF (revised November 2026): 'Wage rates are effective until the DIR issues new rates, which take effect ten (10) days after the issue date. New rates are typically issued each February and August.' and 'Employer Payments may be provided as direct compensation to the employee (added to the hourly wage) or as contributions to qualifying programs or benefit plans for employees and their dependents.' Derived, not printed: 76.87 + 3.66 = 80.53. Because the $3.66 is an increase 'allocated to wages and/or fringes', the basic rate after it is at least $49.20 and the employer payments at most 27.67 + 3.66 = $31.33; the exact split is not published. The OLSE has not published a rate table for permits issued after 2027-06-30.
rules.correction: Adversarial review 2026-11-25 (sources re-fetched that day): the predetermined increase was described only by its date, and the tool read it as a rate for permits issued from 2027-07-01. The notice says the locked rate includes 'any predetermined increase' and that 'No further wage adjustments will apply to permits issued during this timeframe', so permits issued 2026-10-09 to 2027-06-30 owe the $3.66 from 2027-07-01. Added applies_to_permits_issued, applies_from_work_date, the derived 80.53 total and its split bounds, no_further_adjustments_for_permits_issued_in_period, rate_updates and employer_payments_may_be_paid_as_cash; plain_english rewritten. Every published rate is unchanged.

rules.title: State minimum wage $16.90/hour (2026)
rules.plain_english: Every California employer, no matter how small, must pay at least $16.90 per hour for all hours worked starting January 1, 2026. A higher city or county rate overrides this where the work is done.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Every employer, regardless of the number of employees, shall pay to each employee wages not less than the following: (1) Sixteen dollars and ninety cents ($16.90) per hour for all hours worked, effective January 1, 2026;
rules.notes: Exempt from minimum wage per DLSE FAQ: outside salespersons; parent, spouse or child of the employer; apprentices regularly indentured under the Division of Apprenticeship Standards. Separate higher state rates exist for fast food and health care (not normally construction). Public works projects require prevailing wage instead (separate domain).

rules.title: Higher city/county minimum wage must be paid
rules.plain_english: If the city or county where the employee works has a higher minimum wage than the state, the employer must pay the higher local rate. Many California cities are higher than $16.90.

parameters.rule: required_rate = max(federal_rate, state_rate, local_city_or_county_rate_for_work_location)
parameters.local_rate_list_referenced_by_DLSE: UC Berkeley Labor Center inventory of city and county minimum wages (not an official DIR table)

rules.applies_to: Employers with employees working within a city or county that has its own minimum wage ordinance

rules.quote: if a local entity (city or county) has adopted a higher minimum wage, employees must be paid the local wage where it is higher than the state or federal minimum wage rates.
rules.notes: No local rates were read from official city sources in this pass; a tool must look up the jobsite city/county rate (many adjust each July 1 or January 1). For construction crews moving between jobsites, the rate applies per location where hours are worked (verify each ordinance's coverage threshold, e.g., minimum hours worked in the city).

rules.title: State minimum wage adjusts each year by CPI-W (max 3.5%)
rules.plain_english: The state minimum wage now changes every January 1 based on inflation. It can go up by at most 3.5% in a year and can never go down.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: After the state minimum wage reached $15 an hour, the rate is adjusted annually for inflation based on the national consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers (CPI-W). However, the minimum wage cannot be lowered, even if there is a negative CPI, and the highest raise allowed in any one year is 3.5 percent.
rules.notes: A tool should store rates by effective date and refresh each year from MW-20XX orders published by DIR.

rules.title: Minimum wage applies to all hours in each payroll period, including piece rate
rules.plain_english: For every pay period, total pay must equal at least minimum wage times all hours worked, whether the worker is paid hourly, by the piece (e.g., per square or linear foot) or by commission.
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Every employer shall pay to each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise.
rules.notes: Piece-rate workers also have separate rest/recovery and nonproductive time pay rules (Labor Code 226.2) that were not read in this pass.

rules.title: Learner rate: 85% of minimum wage for first 160 hours (not for Wage Order 16 field workers)
rules.plain_english: Under the IWC wage orders that have a learner clause (for example Order 4, which covers office staff), a new worker with no similar experience may be paid 85% of the minimum wage, rounded to the nearest nickel, for their first 160 hours only. Wage Order 16, which covers on-site construction workers, has no learner rate, so field employees must get the full minimum wage from day one.

parameters.source_orders: IWC Orders 1-15 §4(A) (verified in Order 4-2001); absent from Order 16-2001 and MW-2026

rules.applies_to: New employees with no previous similar or related experience who are covered by an IWC order that contains a learner clause (Orders 1-15, e.g., Order 4 office/clerical staff of a contractor). NOT available for on-site construction, drilling, logging or mining employees covered by IWC Order 16-2001.
rules.citation: IWC Orders 1-15 §4(A) learner clause (e.g., IWC Order 4-2001 §4(A)); DLSE Minimum Wage FAQ Q4. Not in IWC Order 16-2001 §4 or MW-2026.
rules.quote: There is an exception for learners, regardless of age, who may be paid not less than 85 percent of the minimum wage rounded to the nearest nickel during their first 160 hours of employment in occupations in which they have no previous similar or related experience.
rules.notes: Derived rate: 16.90 x 0.85 = 14.365, rounded to nearest nickel = $14.35. Local ordinances may not allow a learner rate; check locally. Verification: WO16 §4(A)-(B) and MW-2026 have no learner clause; Order 4-2001 §4(A) does.
rules.correction: The learner subminimum is in the industry wage orders that contain a learner clause (e.g., IWC Order 4 §4(A)), not in MW-2026. IWC Order 16-2001, which covers on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining, has no learner clause in §4. A construction tool must not apply the 85% rate to WO16 field employees. Corrected the citation, source_location, applies_to and plain_english, and added not_available_under_wage_order_16. The 85%, 160-hour and nearest-nickel figures and the $14.35 derivation are confirmed. Rewording 2026-11-27: title reworded to match this correction; no value changed.

rules.title: Exempt (EAP) salary must be at least 2x minimum wage ($70,304/yr in 2026)

parameters.primarily_means: more than one-half of work time

rules.applies_to: Executive, administrative and professional employees of construction/drilling/logging/mining employers
rules.quote: No person shall be considered to be employed in an administrative, executive, or professional capacity unless the person is primarily engaged in the duties which meet the test of the exemption, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to not less than two (2) times the state minimum wage for full-time employment.
rules.notes: Dollar figures are computed from the primary rule and the $16.90 state rate (local minimum wages do not change the state exemption threshold). Duties test also required.

rules.title: Employer provides tools unless worker earns 2x minimum wage

rules.notes: Threshold computed from the $16.90 state minimum wage; whether a higher local minimum wage changes the 2x threshold was not verified. Labor Code 2802 expense reimbursement (vehicle, phone) still applies.

rules.title: Maximum meal and lodging credits against minimum wage (2026)
rules.plain_english: An employer may count meals or lodging toward minimum wage only with a voluntary written agreement, and only up to set amounts (for 2026: breakfast $6.10, lunch $8.42, dinner $11.28; private room $79.46/week).

max_credits_2026_usd.apartment_rule: two-thirds of ordinary rental value, not more than max

rules.title: Overtime 1.5x after 8 hours/day, 40 hours/week, and first 8 hours of 7th day

parameters.hours_counted: hours actually worked (paid sick/holiday hours not worked do not count)

rules.quote: Double the employee's regular rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of 12 hours in any workday and for all hours worked in excess of eight on the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek.

rules.title: How to compute the regular rate for overtime
rules.plain_english: Overtime is paid on the 'regular rate', which includes hourly pay plus shift differentials, piece pay, commissions and non-discretionary bonuses. With two or more rates in a week, use a weighted average; for non-exempt salaried workers divide weekly salary by 40.

parameters.multiple_rates: regular_rate = total_week_earnings / total_week_hours (including OT hours); OT premium added on top
parameters.flat_sum_nondiscretionary_bonus: bonus / maximum legal regular hours in bonus period, then 1.5x or 2x for OT hours
parameters.production_bonus: bonus / total hours worked in period; add 0.5x (or 1x for double time) per OT hour
excluded: pay for non-working time (vacation, holiday, illness)
parameters.floor: regular rate may never be less than applicable minimum wage

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 510; IWC Order 16-2001 §3(A)(1)(c); DLSE Overtime FAQ Q1, Q3, Q4
rules.quote: If you are paid two or more rates by the same employer during the workweek, the regular rate is the "weighted average" which is determined by dividing your total earnings for the workweek, including earnings during overtime hours, by the total hours worked during the workweek, including the overtime hours.
rules.notes: Meal/rest premiums are paid at the 'regular rate of compensation' (Ferra v. Loews, 2021 - case law, not read here).

rules.title: Overtime may be paid on the next regular payday
rules.plain_english: Overtime earned in one pay period must be paid no later than the payday for the next regular pay period. Straight-time wages cannot be delayed.

parameters.wage_statement_correction: OT hours may be recorded as a correction on the next itemized statement with the dates corrected

rules.quote: Overtime wages must be paid no later than the payday for the next regular payroll period following the payroll period in which the overtime wages were earned.

rules.title: All hours 'suffered or permitted' must be paid, even unauthorized overtime
rules.plain_english: If the employer knew or should have known the employee was working, the time must be paid, including overtime that was not approved. The employer may discipline for breaking the policy but must still pay. Overtime pay cannot be waived.

parameters.hours_worked_definition: time subject to employer control, including all time suffered or permitted to work (WO16 §2(J))

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 1194; IWC Order 16-2001 §2(J); DLSE Overtime FAQ Q2, Q9
rules.quote: California's wage and hour laws require that the employee be compensated for any hours he or she is "suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so."
rules.notes: Relevant to timekeeping checks: pre-shift tailgate meetings, yard time and loading tools are typically hours worked when required by the employer.

rules.title: Alternative workweek: up to 10 regular hours/day in construction
rules.plain_english: With a properly adopted alternative workweek schedule, construction employees can work up to 10 hours a day (within 40 hours a week) without daily overtime. Hours beyond the schedule or over 40 still get 1.5x, and over 12 hours gets 2x.

parameters.ot_1_5x: hours beyond regularly scheduled AWS hours and over 40/week
parameters.ot_2x: over 12 hours/day and over 8 hours on days beyond the regularly scheduled workdays
parameters.public_works: AWS requiring >8 hours/day may not be used on public works in violation of Labor Code 1810-1815

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: The alternative workweek schedule shall provide for work by the affected employees of no longer than ten (10) hours per day within a 40 hour workweek without the payment to the affected employees of an overtime rate of compensation pursuant to this section.
rules.notes: Valid only if adopted by the election procedure in WO16 §3(C).

rules.title: Alternative workweek adoption and repeal election steps
rules.plain_english: To adopt an alternative workweek, the employer must propose it in writing, hold disclosure meetings at least 14 days before, win a secret ballot by two-thirds of the work unit, wait 30 days before requiring the new hours, and report the results to DIR within 30 days and post them at the jobsite.

parameters.approval_vote: at least 2/3 of affected employees in the work unit
parameters.ballot: secret ballot during regular hours at work site, before work is performed
parameters.report_to: DIR Office of the Director - Research, P.O. Box 420603, San Francisco, CA 94142-0603
parameters.work_unit: all nonexempt employees of one employer within a given craft who share a common work site

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: adopted in a secret ballot election, held before the performance of work, by at least a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees in the work unit.
rules.notes: Failure to make the written disclosure/meetings makes the election null and void. Do not send ballots to DIR; only results.

rules.title: No discipline for refusing more than 72 hours in a workweek
rules.plain_english: An employee cannot be fired or disciplined for refusing to work more than 72 hours in a workweek, except in a genuine emergency.

parameters.exception: emergency = unpredictable or unavoidable occurrence at unscheduled intervals requiring immediate action (WO16 §2(F))

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: No employee shall be terminated, disciplined or otherwise discriminated against for refusing to work more than 72 hours in any workweek, except in an emergency as defined in Section 2(F) above.

rules.title: Employee-requested makeup time: no daily OT up to 11 hours
rules.plain_english: If an employee asks in writing to make up time lost for a personal obligation in the same workweek, the makeup hours do not trigger daily overtime unless the day goes over 11 hours or the week over 40.
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001) (also applies under CBA unless CBA says otherwise)
rules.quote: the hours of that makeup work time, if performed in the same workweek in which the work time was lost, may not be counted toward computing the total number of hours worked in a day for purposes of the overtime requirements, except for hours in excess of 11 hours of work in one (1) day or forty (40) hours of work in one (1) workweek.

rules.title: One day's rest in seven (may accumulate in construction)
rules.plain_english: Employees are entitled to one day of rest in seven. In construction, rest days may be accumulated when the job reasonably requires 7+ straight days, but each calendar month must still include the equivalent of one day off in seven. Employees cannot be disciplined for refusing the 7th day.

parameters.accumulation_allowed: when nature of employment reasonably requires 7+ consecutive days

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 551-552; IWC Order 16-2001 §3(G); DLSE Overtime FAQ Q6
rules.quote: in each calendar month, the employee shall receive the equivalent of one (1) day’s rest in seven (7).
rules.notes: Seventh-consecutive-day overtime rates still apply.

rules.title: Union CBA exemption from overtime/meal rules requires pay 30% above minimum wage
rules.plain_english: Wage Order 16 overtime, alternative workweek and meal period sections do not apply to employees under a valid union agreement that sets wages, hours and conditions, pays premium rates for all overtime, and pays at least 30% more than the state minimum wage ($21.97/hour in 2026).

still_applies: §3(F) makeup time unless CBA says otherwise
§5 reporting time unless CBA says otherwise
requirements: valid CBA expressly providing wages, hours of work and working conditions
premium wage rates for all overtime hours

rules.applies_to: Union-represented construction employees
rules.quote: if the agreement provides premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked and a regular hourly rate of pay for those employees of not less than thirty (30) percent more than the state minimum wage. (See Labor Code Section 514).

rules.title: 30-minute meal period before end of 5th hour
rules.plain_english: An employee working more than 5 hours must get an uninterrupted, duty-free 30-minute meal period starting no later than the end of the 5th hour. It can be waived by mutual consent only if the whole day is 6 hours or less.

parameters.latest_start: end of 5th hour of work (before start of 6th hour)
parameters.required_to_stay_on_premises: then meal period must be paid

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: No employer shall employ any person for a work period of more than five (5) hours without a meal period of not less than thirty (30) minutes, except that when a work period of not more than six (6) hours will complete the day’s work the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of employer and employee.
rules.notes: Timing rule (end of 5th/10th hour) is from the DLSE Meal Periods FAQ citing Brinker (2012). Unpaid if fully relieved of duty.

rules.title: Second 30-minute meal period before end of 10th hour
rules.plain_english: An employee working more than 10 hours must get a second 30-minute meal period starting by the end of the 10th hour. It can be waived only if the day is 12 hours or less and the first meal was not waived.
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: An employer may not employ an employee for a work period of more than ten (10) hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total hours worked is no more than twelve (12) hours, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent of employer and employee only if the first meal period was not waived.

rules.title: On-duty (paid) meal period needs written, revocable agreement
rules.plain_english: A paid on-the-job meal period is allowed only if the nature of the work truly prevents relief from all duty and there is a written agreement that the employee can revoke in writing at any time.

parameters.test: objective: any employee in that job would be prevented from being relieved of all duty

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 512; IWC Order 16-2001 §10(D); DLSE Meal Periods FAQ
rules.quote: An “on duty” meal period shall be permitted only when the nature of the work prevents employee from being relieved of all duty and when, by written agreement between the parties, an on-the-job paid meal period is agreed to and complies with Labor Code Section 512.
rules.notes: The revocation-in-writing statement requirement is stated in the DLSE Meal Periods FAQ.

rules.title: Missed meal period: 1 extra hour of pay per workday
rules.plain_english: If a compliant meal period is not provided, the employer owes the employee one additional hour of pay at the regular rate of compensation for that workday.

parameters.unit: per workday the meal period is not provided

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: If an employer fails to provide an employee a meal period in accordance with the applicable provisions of this order, the employer shall pay the employee one (1) hour of pay at the employee’s regular rate of compensation for each workday that the meal period is not provided.
rules.notes: DLSE: premium is not hours worked for OT and has a 3-year limitations period (Murphy v. Kenneth Cole). DLSE late-payment FAQ: premiums are wages subject to Labor Code 210 (Naranjo 2022). Where a CBA has a final and binding dispute mechanism for meal periods, the CBA prevails.

rules.title: Paid 10-minute rest break per 4 hours or major fraction
rules.plain_english: Employees get a paid, duty-free 10-minute rest break for every 4 hours worked or major fraction (more than 2 hours). No break is required if the day is under 3.5 hours. Typical: 3.5-6 hours = 1 break, over 6-10 = 2, over 10-14 = 3.

parameters.formula: if h < 3.5: 0 else floor(h/4) + (1 if (h - 4*floor(h/4)) > 2 else 0)
parameters.timing: insofar as practicable in the middle of each work period

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: IWC Order 16-2001 §11(A),(C); DLSE Rest Periods FAQ
rules.quote: The authorized rest period time shall be based on the total hours worked daily at the rate of ten (10) minutes net rest time for every four (4) hours worked, or major fraction thereof.
rules.notes: 'Major fraction' = more than 2 hours per DLSE Rest Periods FAQ. Rest periods need not be recorded (WO16 §6(A)(1)). CBA providing equivalent protection is exempt (§11(E)).

rules.title: Construction: rest breaks may be staggered and taken at the immediate work area
rules.plain_english: Construction employers may stagger rest breaks or schedule them to match natural breaks in the work, and may designate the employee's immediate work area as the rest location.

parameters.rest_location: employer-designated areas, may include or be limited to the immediate work area

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Nothing in this provision shall prevent an employer from staggering rest periods to avoid interruption in the flow of work and to maintain continuous operations, or from scheduling rest periods to coincide with breaks in the flow of work that occur in the course of the workday.
rules.notes: Employees must still be relieved of all duty during the break (Augustus v. ABM, per DLSE FAQ).

rules.title: Missed rest break for continuous operations: make up same day or pay 10 minutes same pay period
rules.plain_english: If stopping would jeopardize the product or process (e.g., a continuous concrete pour), the rest break can be skipped, but it must be made up the same workday or the 10 minutes must be paid at the regular rate in the same pay period.

parameters.condition: limited circumstances where disruption of continuous operations would jeopardize the product or process

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Rest periods need not be authorized in limited circumstances when the disruption of continuous operations would jeopardize the product or process of the work. However, the employer shall make up the missed rest period within the same workday or compensate the employee for the missed ten (10) minutes of rest time at his/her regular rate of pay within the same pay period.

rules.title: Missed rest break(s): 1 extra hour of pay per workday
rules.plain_english: If any required rest break is not authorized and permitted, the employer owes one additional hour of pay at the regular rate for that workday (one hour per day, not per missed break).
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Thus, if an employer does not provide all of the rest periods required in a workday, the employee is entitled to one additional hour of pay for that workday, not one additional hour of pay for each rest period that was not provided during that workday.
rules.notes: A day with both a missed meal and missed rest break can carry two premiums (one each) - case law, not read here.

rules.title: Construction sites must provide potable water, soap and single-use towels for hand washing
rules.plain_english: Construction employers must supply enough drinkable water, soap (or similar cleanser) and single-use towels for hand washing. Unlike other wage orders, a designated eating place is not required.

required_items: adequate supply of potable water
soap or other suitable cleansing agent
single use towels

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: In all places of employment the employer shall provide an adequate supply of potable water, soap, or other suitable cleansing agent and single use towels for hand washing.
rules.notes: Cal/OSHA sanitation and drinking water rules (Title 8) add further requirements (safety domain).

rules.title: Lactation break time and space; $100/day citation
rules.plain_english: Employers must give reasonable break time and a suitable space to express breast milk. Denial can cost one hour of premium pay per violation and a $100-per-day citation.

parameters.break_time: reasonable, each time needed; runs concurrently with rest breaks if possible
parameters.extra_break_time_paid: not required if beyond authorized rest time

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: BOFE may issue a citation for one hundred dollars ($100) for each day an employee is denied reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk.
rules.notes: Space requirements for construction sites (Labor Code 1031) not read in this pass.

rules.title: Missed heat-illness cool-down (recovery) period: 1 hour premium pay
rules.plain_english: A 'recovery period' is a cool-down break to prevent heat illness. If an employer fails to provide one required by a Cal/OSHA standard, it owes one extra hour of pay at the regular rate for that workday, and cool-down time is paid time.

parameters.trigger: recovery period required by Cal/OSHA standard (e.g., 8 CCR 3395) not provided

rules.applies_to: Employers with outdoor (and indoor heat) workers covered by Cal/OSHA heat illness standards, including construction
rules.source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.7 (not fetched; blocked) - text seen only in search excerpts
rules.quote: "recovery period" means a cooldown period afforded an employee to prevent heat illness.
rules.notes: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov blocked automated fetching; quote and premium rule taken from search-result excerpts of Labor Code 226.7 and law-firm summaries. Verify the current statute text.

rules.title: Allow and encourage cool-down rest in shade (at least 5 minutes)
rules.plain_english: Outdoor workers must be allowed and encouraged to take a cool-down rest in the shade of at least 5 minutes whenever they feel they need it, and must be monitored during it.

parameters.trigger: whenever the worker feels the need to protect from overheating
parameters.symptoms_observed: do not order back to work; observe until symptoms abate; provide first aid/EMS

rules.applies_to: All outdoor places of employment, including construction sites
rules.quote: The employer is required to allow and encourage workers to take a cool-down rest in the shade for a period of no less than five minutes at a time when they feel the need to do so to protect themselves from overheating.
rules.notes: Shade/temperature triggers and full heat-plan duties belong to the Cal/OSHA safety domain. Page dated June 2024.

rules.title: Construction is a high-heat industry: extra procedures at 95°F
rules.plain_english: When it is 95°F or hotter, construction employers must follow Cal/OSHA's additional high-heat procedures (e.g., observation, pre-shift meetings).

industries: Transportation/delivery of agricultural products and of construction or other heavy materials

rules.applies_to: Outdoor construction employers
rules.quote: In addition, the following industries are subject to additional requirements in high heat (temperature that equals or exceeds 95 F)
rules.notes: Construction is listed as one of the industries on the same page. Details of 3395(e) procedures belong to the Cal/OSHA domain.

rules.title: Reporting time pay: half the scheduled day, minimum 2 and maximum 4 hours
